speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO PROPOSED SYSTEM OF RATIONING EFFECTIVE APRIL 1
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply if he is prepared to make a statement on Canada's gasoline rationing system, which it was announced some weeks ago was to go into effect on April 1. If not to-day, when may the house and the country expect a statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO PROPOSED SYSTEM OF RATIONING EFFECTIVE APRIL 1
speechtext: Preparations for the rationing of gasoline are proceeding, with the intention of bringing it into force on April 1. The need for this rationing is becoming more apparent every day as additional tanker tonnage is sunk along our coast and as the demands of the army services increase. The details will be announced shortly by the oil controller. It is a highly involved matter, and while I could bring the information to the house I think the purpose would be served equally well by the oil controller explaining the situation through the public press. I discussed the matter with him this morning, and I know it is his intention to take such action within the next day or two. If my hon. friend so desires I shall be glad to get the release and present it to the house before it is given 'to the press.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF ORDER TO EASTERN SECTION OF CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPLICATION OF ORDER TO EASTERN SECTION OF CANADA
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to
the Secretary of State. It has reference to the question of daylight saving. I should like to explain at the outset that I am not personally opposed to daylight saving, but in view of the situation as I understand it in eastern Canada I believe this question should be asked.
On Monday, Janua^ 26, order in council P.C. 547 was passed under the provisions of the War Measures Act, whereby it was ordered that as from Monday, February 9 next, until otherwise ordered, the time for all purposes in Canada shall be one hour in advance of accepted standard time. The order recites that on September 20, 1940, daylight saving time was continued for the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and that the Secretary of State reported that it would be advantageous to the war effort of Canada to have daylight saving time observed in all the time zones in Canada.-
May I point out to the Secretary of State that the major part of that portion of Canada within the Atlantic standard time zone- roughly speaking, the portion of Canada lying east of the international boundary at the Saint Croix river-is now thirty-six minutes, as at Saint John, New Brunswick-ahead of true sun time; and to have Atlantic daylightsaving time imposed in that zone will put practically all the people of New Brunswick, and a great portion of the people' of Nova Scotia, ninety-six minutes ahead of true sun time. When the terms of the order were being considered, was any consideration given to that position? To-day we are in the happy position of substantially conserving daylight by thirty-six minutes, and are operating on the same time as the large central provinces, which is most convenient. It may be that 44561-9
other factors, such as transportation problems, time tables, and so on, affect the position; but as at present advised I suggest that the position be reviewed so far as it relates to the maritime provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State):
subtopic: APPLICATION OF ORDER TO EASTERN SECTION OF CANADA
speechtext: The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) was good enough to give me notice of the question he has just asked. Unfortunately I have not had sufficient time to go into the technical matter he has raised, namely, the application of the order to certain sections operating on Atlantic standard time. There is one matter he suggests, however, which, I believe, cannot possibly be correct, namely, that whereas the western boundary of the zone of that portion of the maritimes which is on Atlantic standard time is thirty-six minutes faster than sun time, that condition would apply wholly throughout the maritimes.

speechtext:
It is
because we are nearer that meridian. It goes out into the sea.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF ORDER TO EASTERN SECTION OF CANADA

subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a further question, directed to the Minister of Finance, and based upon order in council P.C. 394, dated January 20, 1942-just last week. This order in council, which was passed on the minister's recommendation, provides for the exemption from customs duties and war exchange tax of anthracite coal when imported into the maritime provinces between January 1 and April 30, 1942. I should like to ask the minister the reasons for the passing of this order in council, the reasons for restricting its operation to the maritime provinces, and also whether it is not anticipated that this exemption will discriminate against the coal producers and coal miners of the maritimes. May I ask also why this exemption, which expressly suspends a provision of an act of parliament, was made by order in council

Anthracite Goal

one day before the session was resumed? Why was it not brought before parliament in the usual and proper manner?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I counted correctly, the leader of the opposition has asked four questions. I shall proceed to answer them.
He asks first why there has been an exemption of anthracite from customs duties on coal entering the maritime provinces. The reason is that the freight on anthracite moving by water is very much greater than it was a few months ago. If importers of anthracite coal are to be able to continue to sell anthracite under the price ceiling, something will have to be done for them. Assistance could be given to them either by way of subsidy or by way of tax or tariff remission. It was decided that tariff remission would amount to about the proper sum to enable them to continue to sell under the price ceiling. The same necessity does not exist in the case of anthracite into other parts of Canada, because it does not move by water as it does into the maritime provinces.	'

subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext: It does not all move by water to the maritimes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext:
Pretty much. This applies only to anthracite moving by ship, waterborne coal which comes to seaports. It was considered it would be perfectly practicable to limit the concession to the maritime provinces, because there would be no danger of this coal coming into the martime provinces and then being loaded on cars and shipped to other parts of Canada.
With regard to any possible prejudice to producers of coal in the maritime provinces, as the hon. member knows, no hard coal is produced there.

subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext: I believe anthracite will be no more dangerous as a competitive factor in the coal situation now than it was before, when the ocean rates were so much lower than they are to-day.

subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext: The fifty cents duty has kept some out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXEMPTION FROM CUSTOMS DUTIES AND WAR EXCHANGE TAX WHEN IMPORTED INTO MARITIMES
speechtext:
Oh, yes, but freights were very much lower when the fifty cents was imposed.
With regard to the final question, as to why it was done by order in council, I would point out that it was done in that way pursuant either to the War Measures Act or to the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act; I am not sure which. Anyway, there was ample

statutory authority for proceeding, and it was done by order in council because it had to be done. If we had brought it before parliament on the first day of the session we would not have reached it for a long time. I do not know what else we could have done, because it was a budgetary sort of thing, and action could not be deferred until the spring or early summer. It had to be done right away.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Alphonse Fournier for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before beginning my address I should like to read two telegrams which I have just received. The first is from Mr. Lidstone, secretary of the Toronto business men's branch of the Canadian Legion. It reads:
Toronto business men's branch of the Canadian Legion in meeting strongly urge you to oppose plebiscite and to support legion policy of total war effort including conscription for overseas service.
The other is from Colonel C. E. Reynolds, president of the Canadian Corps Association It reads:
I ask you to request our Prime Minister to beg Churchill, Wavell and Prime Minister Curtin to hang on. Canada is voting in three months.
After listening to the excellent speeches of the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I could not help but regret that I too had not had the advantage of a legal training. May I congratulate them both upon the presentation of their cases. On the day that the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) spoke the press reported that both the Kiwanis club and the local council of women of Brantford had passed resolutions disapproving the proposed plebiscite. In addition the Brantford trades and labour council is reported to have wired the member expressing their disapproval. I venture to say that if he has had anything like the overwhelming mail I have had from my constituents he knows the extent of the support for compulsory selective service in his own riding. I think I am justified in saying that when the hon. member spoke on Friday last he was speaking as a supporter of the government rather than in his capacity of representative of those who elected him. I presume he spoke again for the government when he said, as reported on page 16 of Hansard:
Man-power for our army is not now our most pressing need.
If man-power for the army is not so urgent, why did the district commanding officer of military district No. 1, London, Ontario, write on January 6, 1942, to a married man with three children who had been rejected three times as unfit for service and put in category E, as follows:
1.	Some time ago you offered your services for enlistment into the Canadian active army but were rejected as being medically unfit.
2.	Recently, medical categories have been revised very materially and some causes for rejection completely eliminated.
3.	Your previous offer of service is appreciated and as the need for men 's now urgent, it is suggested you would wish to take advantage of this opportunity to have your medical status reviewed.
4.	If such is the case, would you be good enough to present yourself at Wolseley barracks, London, or St. Luke's barracks, Windsor, at your earliest convenience.
5.	If you have no way of getting to London, please advise this office or your nearest armoury, and an effort will be made to provide transportation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I ask my hon. friend to whom that letter was addressed?
The Address-Mr. Bruce

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The man does not want his name announced. This is the original paper from the recruiting officer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend must know that he has no right to use communications in the house unless he is prepared to give full particulars of any name that will authenticate the document.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: For obvious reasons this man does not wish his name revealed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: If my hon. friend cannot give the name, then he has no right to use the communication.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not propose to give his name.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The other day the Prime Minister gave the figure for our active army as 260,000. I am reliably informed that of the so-called active army, at least 60,000 men are not available because they are employed as home guards or on the staffs of training establishments or hospitals. Surely it is improper to include those men. I should like also to call attention to the fact that in our coast defence forces we have many men who are known as "R" recruits, men who have been called up under the mobilization act but have failed to volunteer for overseas service. In my judgment it is a misrepresentation to suggest that those men are active service units.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that they are not included in the number on active service.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of course I accept the
minister's statement. In reply to a question which I asked yesterday as to whether units of the sixth division would be available to go to the assistance of the United States if they were attacked, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said in part, as reported on page 109 of Hansard:
I want to say to him, however, that the units of these brigade groups would be available if it were considered advisable and necessary to send men to the United States, less any home defence personnel who were in those units who did not volunteer for that duty.
In other words, the commanding officer of these units would take his troops to the United States boundary, call a halt, and ask all "R" recruits to take three paces to the rear and drop out, since he could not ask them to serve outside Canada. If amongst these units there were several signallers, the line of communication would be put into confusion and our force rendered useless. Can anyone imagine a more ridiculous or perilous position for our troops to occupy? Would Great Britain be mobilizing

her women if she had not reached the limit of her resources in man-power? Would United States troops be landing in Ireland if manpower was not needed by Britain?
I am not unmindful of the contribution which has already been made by our factories and our shipyards and of the splendid part labour has played, and I wish to commend all concerned, which includes, of course, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) for what he and they have achieved. But speaking as one who is trying to run a farm I have the greatest sympathy and admiration for the farmers who- are still carrying on, producing foodstuffs in spite of the low prices and steadily mounting wages and the increasing difficulty in getting labour at all. Unless something is done for them it will have a serious effect on our food production programme-if we have one.
The hon. member for Brantford City compared our war effort with that of the United States. My answer to that comparison will be brief. The United States brought in universal compulsory selective service as soon as she declared war, and according to Mr. Winant, the United States Ambassador to Britain, speaking in London yesterday, the United States is now planning to have an army, not of 3,600,000, but of 7,000,000. The United States is preparing to attack; Canada is waiting to be attacked. Can anyone imagine a more humiliating position for any country to be in at this time of crisis, when within a few weeks the fury of the enemy will be descending upon us, to have its Prime Minister, knowing full well the needs after nearly two and a half years of war, transfer his responsibility to an uninformed electorate? When I heard the member for Brantford City supporting his chief, in spite of his declaration only a few days before that he was in favour of compulsory selective service, it reminded me of the story of another Macdonald, a Macdonald of revered memory at least on this side of the house. On one occasion when Doctor George Grant, then Principal of Queen's university, told Sir John A. Macdonald that he always supported him when he was right, Sir John replied: "The kind of support I prefer is that which is given me when I am wrong." Such a loyal supporter as the member for Brantford City' must be appreciated at this time.
Referring to his western tour last August, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as reported at page 47 of this session's Hansard, said:
At the time of my tour of western Canada, prior to my visit to Britain, an attempt was made to raise the issue of conscription. A cloud no larger than a man's hand appeared in

the political sky at Calgary and in some other of the western cities. I at once recognized that this was not due to a spontaneous movement on the part of the people themselves, but was rather the manifestation of a political movement carefully organized by opponents of the government, to force conscription to the fore as a political issue.
I wonder if the cloud to which he refers would not have been larger if his vision on emerging from the train had not been obscured by a large banner stretching across the street calling for conscription. The hostile reception which he received in that city, plus the selection of a new leader by the Conservative party and his immediate announcement of policy, plus the recent activities of an Ontario committee for total war, are given as reasons by the Prime Minister why he finds it expedient to have a plebiscite. But then he went on to say that the place to fight out this question is on the floor of the house. And later on he announced the plebiscite. I must confess that I am unable to follow his argument.
In his speech the other day the Prime Minister also said, at page 48 of Hansard:
Outside parliament altogether, the political skies have now become so overcast with controversy, promoted by high-pressure methods and highly financed publicity, that the nature and extent of Canada's war effort is not only being obscured, but is in danger of being seriously impaired.
No doubt the Prime Minister refers to the recent movement in the province of Ontario for total war by the immediate enforcement of unrestricted compulsory selective service. When the Prime Minister uses the term "political pressure," he means by that, I presume, pressure from his political enemies. Would he put Mr. C. L. Burton in this category, or Mr. James Y. Murdoch? I think I am correct in saying that they are both life-long Liberals, yet they were joint chairmen with Mr. F. K. Morrow, a patriotic citizen and a prominent Roman Catholic whose name will be found in every philanthropic organization. The committee was strictly non-partisan and represented practically every social and patriotic organization in the province. May I refer to just a few members of that committee?
There was Mrs. Wallace Campbell, president of the Ontario division of the Red Cross and dominion chairman of the Red Cross women's war work committee. I should like to pay tribute to the outstanding contribution made by Mrs. Campbell to Canada's war effort by the wonderful leadership she has given to many thousands of women throughout Canada. Other members of the committee were Mrs. W. B. Horkins, dominion president of the Imperial Order of Daughters
The Address-Mr. Bruce
of the Empire; and Mrs. H. D. Warren, dominion commissioner of the Girl Guides of Canada; Mrs. Maud Miller, Ontario president of the Provincial Council of Women; Dr. W. E. Gallie, dean of the Medical Faculty of the University of Toronto; Dr. H. J. Cody, president of the University of Toronto; Bishop R. J. Renison, rector of St. Paul's Anglican Church, Toronto; Commissioner Orames of the Salvation Army; Sir Ernest MacMillan, president of the Toronto Symphony Orchestra; Hon. Mr. Biggs, a former minister of the Farmer-Liberal government of Ontario, Mr. Aubrey Davis, Mr. Elmer Davis, Mr. William Dry den, and Doctor Smirle Lawson, chief coroner for Ontario.
Do these names suggest political enemies of the Prime Minister and the Liberal party? I ask the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenize).
In referring to the work of this group of patriotic citizens, the Prime Minister speaks of the controversy being "promoted by high pressure methods and high financed publicity." What about the government's own political publicity advertising? What about the pamphlets, speeches and other things which are distributed, we are told, to 400,000 people?
I listened most carefully to the long and laboured effort of the Prime Minister on Monday last to justify the course he is taking. He failed miserably in his attempt to convince the public, as is evidenced in reading editorial comments and letters in the press.
I think I have shown that this demand for compulsory selective service comes not alone from Conservatives but from many of the Prime Minister's own personal Liberal friends. Does he not realize that it arises from a growing feeling of apprehension due to the extension of the war to this continent? Remember that the call from Ontario for conscription for a total war came after Japan's entry into the war.
Although the Prime Minister speaks of having first heard of this subject when he went west, may I remind him that I proposed it several months before in this house, and for my pains was severely rebuked by the Minister of National Defence.
In my opinion it is criminal folly, both from the standpoint of delay and that of dividing the country in the face of the enemy, for the government to hold a plebiscite at this time. How humiliated we must feel that recent events have justified the cartoon in the Montreal Gazette of January 23, wherein the Prime Minister is portrayed as a fireman in charge of the hose in front of a great conflagration, saying to his helper who is about to turn on the water hydrant, "Let's take a vote
The Address-Mr. Bruce

to see if we should turn it on full." Many of you have seen this cartoon; I do not suppose it will be reproduced in Hansard.
May I .say again to the Prime Minister that conscription was not an issue in the last campaign. How could it have been an issue when both leaders were in agreement? To make it an issue, surely one party must oppose what the other proposes. I had no occasion during my election campaign to refer to or make any commitment on the subject of conscription. The question then was whether the country would trust the present government to carry on the war, and the argument which the electorate apparently accepted was that it would be better that they should do so rather than change horses in crossing a stream. One of their slogans, I would remind the house, was "King or Chaos." We now have both.
The Prime Minister emphasized again his oft-repeated claim of preserving national unity. While I agree with the importance of this I am not in agreement with his method of bringing it about. In my view there is nothing which would promote national unity more than equality of service and of sacrifice for all; and per contra, there is nothing that would bring about a greater feeling of bitterness and disharmony than the knowledge that some sections of the community were bearing a greater share of the burdens and dangers in the fighting forces than others. There is nothing which will bring people more closely together than to share intimately and equally in danger and sacrifice.
Enjoyment of the privileges of citizenship in Canada carries with it the obligation upon all of defending their country'. I do not -mean that all available youth should necessarily go overseas to fight, but by compulsory selective service they would be placed either on farms, in the factories, or in the forces, wherever their special abilities would be most useful.
, Immediately following the Prime Minister's speech we had in this house striking evidence of disunity among his followers, and this in spite of the Prime Minister's announcement, following his three-hour caucus a few days ago, that "we have never had such a united and enthusiastic meeting". If this could be described as a "love-feast", what must the others have been like! I wonder what kind of "love-feast" they had at their caucus this morning.
I desire to commend the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray), as I know his constituents will do, for the courageous, manly course he took in following his conscience rather than the crack of the party whip. When he goes back home and faces his people he will be able to hold his head erect, knowing that he has faithfully done his duty.
fUr. Bruce.]
Already the much-advertised unity of the Liberals shows three serious cracks. And, forsooth, we are to have yet another French-Canadian party, led by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe).
The hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle) quoted a passage from my speech of last November, and from his remarks I take it that he did not know the meaning of compulsory selective service, which I thought I had made clear in June last. I will let one of his own countrymen reply to what he said in the house two days ago. I am going to quote from an open letter written by Captain Talbot M. Papineau, headed as follows:	"In the
Field, France, March 21st, 1916", and addressed to his uncle, Henri Bourassa, in which he says:
Those of us in this great army who may be so fortunate as to return to our Canada will have faced the grimmest and sincerest issues of life and death. We will have experienced the unhappy strength of brute force. We will have seen our loved comrades die in blood and suffering. Beware lest we return with revengeful feelings; for I say to you that from those who, while we fought and suffered here, remained in safety and comfort in Canada and failed to give us encouragement and support, as well as from those who grew fat with wealth dishonorably gained by political graft and by dishonest business methods at our expense, we shall demand a heavy day of reckoning.
We shall inflict upon them the punishment they deserve, not by physical violence, for we shall have had enough of that, nor by unconstitutional or illegal means, for we are fighting to protect, not to destroy, justice and freedom, but by the invincible power of our moral influence. Remember, too, that if Canada lias become a nation, respected and self-respecting, she owes it to her citizens who have fought and died in this distant land and not to those self-styled nationalists who have stayed at home
If Captain Papineau had written from our present army overseas he could not have better expressed the situation as it exists today than he did in 1916.
May I suggest to the Prime Minister that there is still another way out. He must already know that it is unnecessary for him to be relieved of his promise by eight of the provinces of Canada; for he knows full well where they stand. The Gallup poll of the whole of Canada was taken by the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion, also the Toronto Star, and twenty-five other prominent newspapers of all shades of editorial belief, at the end of December last. The result was published in the Toronto Star as follows: sixty per cent would vote for selective service overseas; thirty per cent against; and ten per cent undecided or would not vote.
A recent survey by the Globe and Mail, with the cooperation of eighty-one weekly newspapers of the province of Ontario, was

made to test the rural opinion on compulsory selective service anywhere, with the result that ninety-five per cent of the rural papers gave it as their considered opinion that there would be no objection from the farmers to compulsory selective service if the government made provision for farm labour.

What a time for a plebiscite, corresponding as it does with the announced intention of Hitler to launch his spring offensive? The Prime Minister and the party caucus will not escape the shame and humiliation attached to this cowardly decision. After this, how many will be able to hold their heads high before their constituents? Why ' not ask this parliament for a vote, which I feel confident it would certainly give, to absolve the Prime Minister from his improvident undertaking? What justification is there for asking the thousands of Canadians who did not vote for him in the last election to release him from his pledge? They may decline to vote when they realize that this might be improperly interpreted as a vote of confidence in his handling of the war. I think I would myself decline to vote unless the Prime Minister gave a definite undertaking to bring in compulsory selective service if he receives an affirmative vote.
The Prime Minister must know that there is anger and bitter resentment on the part of thousands of Canadians for the humiliating position in which he has placed them. May I suggest that he is taking a very dangerous course which might very well cause the rise of another William Lyon Mackenzie to lead a movement for responsible government.
If the Prime Minister is committed on conscription he is equally committed against a national government; consequently, if he is bound to proceed with a plebiscite he should also ask to be released from his commitment against a national government. We are asked at this time, the most critical time in the history of the world, to spend millions of dollars and delay our war effort-for what? Simply to save the Prime Minister's face- not to save Canada, mark you, but to save the Liberal party. Is it worth the price? On Monday the Prime Minister said, "I am being asked to sell my birthright for their mess of pottage." If by this he means his right to prevent this country from doing its obvious duty of reinforcing our troops overseas by equality of sacrifice, then I say to him that the life of one of our soldiers overseas is of more value than the political life of the Prime Minister.
I invite your attention, Mr. Speaker, particularly to what I am about to say now. We must reinforce our own brave men. Are we going to face the problem of getting recruits with folded hands, by doing nothing? We have asked these gallant men to go to the front, and they are giving their lives for us. Are we going to abandon them now? The government talks as if we were going to support them, but acts as if we were going to abandon them when the reserves are exhausted. I believe the people of Canada have the courage and the patriotism to respond to the need if they are told by the government what the need is.
Parliament is now in session and can enact new measures adequate to the situation if only the government will take hold of things. Surely in a crisis like this, when our men are falling at the front, pouring out their lifeblood this very day that Canada may be free, we are not going to sit silent, in apathy and helplessness. I want to state briefly but definitely my position on this question. We have in the cabinet, I believe, eight hon. gentlemen who are veterans of the last world war, some of whom still carry the marks of the wounds they suffered in that great conflict. Some of these hon. gentlemen have badges which were given them for distinguished valour on the field of battle. Some of them have sons, as many of the rest of us have, in the army, in the navy or in the air force. I know this question has been considered, not just for a day but day after day, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), by those members of the cabinet to whom I have referred, and by the other members of the government as well. They have come to a decision on what they believe to be the best course under the circumstances, and I am prepared to accept their judgment.
That is my first reason for supporting them in their proposal. I do not know why the Prime Minister should be singled out as the only one who has made commitments. Every member of this party, when he accepted the platform laid down by our leaders, by our cabinet, made commitments just as strong as those made by the Prime Minister himself. And for the life of me I cannot understand the position taken now by the hon. member for Parkdale. I believe he accepted the platform that was laid down by his leader, who headed a national government party; and having accepted that platform he made commitments just as strong as those made by his leader. I am in favour of this proposal because it not only relieves the Prime Minister of the commitments he has made but I would say it also relieves all hon. members on both sides of the house, though I cannot speak for the two independent groups, since I do not know what stand they took.
Under the circumstances I think it is the honourable and decent thing to do. I have been in public life in one way or another for some twenty-seven years, and I have always tried to be honest with the people who

elected me. I agree with the government in the action they propose to take now. It is up to the people themselves. If they want to relieve us of those commitments, well and good.
I should like also to take this opportunity to congratulate members of the cabinet upon the manner in which they are carrying on the work of their various departments. Especially do I commend the ministers who have been entrusted with the responsibility of organizing Canada's war effort. These hon. gentlemen are carrying loads such as perhaps few cabinet ministers have ever been called upon to carry. As a supporter of the government I take this opportunity publicly to express my confidence in them. I assure them we appreciate the effort they are putting forth to apply sound business principles in carrying out their task. We realize that if any scandal arose in connection with this tremendous job of prosecuting Canada's war effort, among others, the private members supporting the government would suffer. Therefore we should be grateful that we. have in the cabinet men who stand solidly for honesty and integrity in the great task to which they have set their hands. In the ministers who have been entrusted with the responsibility of organizing our war effort we have a group of men who hold1 our entire confidence and have, I believe, the confidence of the great masses of the people of Canada.
I take this opportunity also of paying what I believe to be a well-deserved tribute to the Prime Minister, who has endeavoured to give us efficient and honest administration. Canada is fortunate at the present time in having at its head a gentleman with the experience, ability and honesty of purpose found in our present leader. It was no surprise to me when he and his government received such splendid endorsation at the last federal election. Notwithstanding, however, that remarkable expression of approval by the people, there were editors of some of our important daily papers who both before and since the beginning of the war have continued their sniping, and who apparently are definitely determined to try to destroy confidence in the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues. I do not complain about constructive criticism, because in my opinion it is the finest thing we can have. Anyone who represents the public will appreciate that kind of criticism. But the kind I have in mind is criticism which is not based on facts, or, as in many cases, criticism based on facts which are grossly misrepresented.
For example, on the occasion of my coming to Ottawa in November, 1940, for the continuation of the adjourned session, before I boarded the train at Toronto I obtained a copy of the Toronto Globe and Mail. One of the first articles which attracted my attention-it was on the front page-stated that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was coming back from overseas empty-handed. It pointed out that he had been unable to come to any agreement with the United Kingdom government for the sale of our farm produce. Just what good was to be accomplished or what useful purpose was to be served by spreading a story such as that across the country at that particular time is something which for the life of me I cannot understand.
A short time ago, I believe about the middle of December, the same paper carried an editorial in which it pictured the Prime Minister holding out a delicious carrot, which represented senatorships, cabinet portfolios, judgeships and the like. It also described private members supporting the government as donkeys, crowding around, trying to get a bite out of the carrot. I would be disposed to say some nasty things about an offensive editorial of that kind-, but I take the view that if they are not ashamed of it, then surely there is nothing I could say which would have any effect on them. In my opinion the Prime Minister has on many occasions been most unjustly and unfairly criticized.
Because of what is happening now I would like to refer to what has happened in the past. We see at the present time an organized effort which hurls a barrage of criticism at the government and the Prime Minister, and which is definitely harming this country's war effort. That is my reason for referring to past events. We well recall the incident in September, 1938. when the position with respect to Czechoslovakia was so acute. On that occasion many of the papers I have in mind persistently demanded that the Prime Minister make a

The Address-Mr. Golding

definite stand, that he should make definite commitments. We were repeatedly told that all the dominions, with the exception of Canada, had done that very thing. A careful review of the proceedings in those other parliaments reveals that not one of them had made any such commitments. This fact was clearly established by the proceedings in the British House of Commons, on the occasion of a question being placed on the order paper in which it was asked if any commitments had been made by any of the dominions. The question was answered by a definite "no" from the then prime minister.
It is also clearly established that Great Britain herself was acting only in the role of mediator at that time, and was particularly anxious that no action be taken or no word be spoken which would prejudice the success of their efforts.
In view of these facts-and they are facts- I have never been able to understand the sense of the tremendous barrage of criticism which was hurled at the government on that occasion. The Prime Minister had stated his position time after time, in parliament and out of it. He said that in the event of a crisis which might involve this country in war, parliament would be assembled, and parliament itself must make the decision on such a momentous question. This promise was kept to the letter, and as a result Canada entered the war a united people. That history is now written, and surely it must be a source of satisfaction to look back and, in the light of all circumstances, appreciate the soundness of the position taken then by the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister has been criticized, too, for not taking a definite stand on important questions. I agree at once that he has not danced to the tune played by some of these super-wise gentlemen who, because they have been entrusted with the responsibility of writing a few editorials, think it is impossible for them under any circumstances whatsoever to err. But he acted at the proper time and in the proper place according to his judgment. I think it is generally conceded that over the period of years that he has been Prime Minister his judgment has been most remarkably sound. When this parliament was assembled on September 7, 1939, under circumstances most serious, the Prime Minister stated his position briefly but definitely-page 21 of Hansard- as follows:
We stand for the defence of Canada; we stand for the cooperation of this country at the side of Great Britain; and if this house will not support us in that policy, it will have to find some other government to assume the responsibilities of the present.

I think it was a source of satisfaction to him when he saw how many members from all sides of the house rallied to his support and to the support of the government by the strong stand they took. From that time in September until January in the following year, the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues endeavoured, by means of radio talks and press releases, to keep the people informed as to what action was being taken to organize our war effort. The radio talks and press releases were appreciated by the great majority of our citizens, but there were those who ridiculed the whole effort as nothing but political propaganda. The situation in which the government found itself at that time was simply this: if they remained silent, they were criticized; if they endeavoured to keep the people informed as to what was being done, that was called cheap political propaganda. It was no wonder, therefore, that the Prime Minister definitely decided to dissolve parliament when we met on January 25, 1940.
It will also be recalled that at that time the Prime Minister was placed by his opponents in the same category as Hitler for having, as they termed it, scuttled parliament. If we will just re-read the brief debate which took place on that occasion we will find that the Prime Minister stated that charges had been made that his government had lost the confidence of the people. Some of those charges were made in places which could not be ignored. He believed that if the Canadian people felt there was another party or group who could manage things better than the government was doing, then they ought to be given the opportunity of voting for that party or group. In view of that democratic statement and that democratic action I could never understand the philosophy of those who placed the Prime Minister in the same category as Hitler. Since when have we heard Hitler tell the German people that if they were not satisfied with his leadership they would be given the opportunity to select someone else to guide their ship of state?
I am not going to review the charges and counter-charges which were thrown back and forth during the last election, but there are some aspects of that whole discusssion which I think should not be overlooked. Every hon. gentleman who was a member of this house in 1939 will recall that a determined effort was put forth by a section of our press to discredit the House of Commons and create want of confidence in every member representing the people at that time. During the election a determined effort was made to destroy confidence in our party system of government. I should like to say a few words in reference to that.

The Address-Mr. Golding
I think we all remember the formation of the "Leadership league" in. the city of Toronto, which league was organized somewhat as the present "total war" committee was. The Leadership league apparently took unto itself the task of trying to improve the position of our people, which was of course a most commendable thing to do. Unfortunately it set out to accomplish that task by carrying on a campaign designed deliberately to create a lack of confidence in every hon. [DOT]member who sat in this house at that time. We were called politicians and the whole trend of their effort seemed to be to make people believe that we were a species of humanity which should be immediately exterminated. Efforts were made to make the people believe that we were not to be trusted. Reading between the lines we could see that we were accused of being far more concerned with the welfare of our parties than we were with the welfare of those who had sent us here to represent them. Efforts were also made to make the people believe that we had all made promises at election time that we had not the slightest intention of even trying to fulfil. That is the sort of campaign that was carried on by this organization against the members of the house at that time, and it was directed at all members.
In reference to this criticism I may say that I have attended quite a number of public meetings in my day, and I have heard those aspiring to office give an outline of the policies they would support if elected. Generally speaking I, think they did that very thing. In view of the criticism which was directed against the members of the house by this organization it is interesting to read the assurances that they themselves were giving, assurances which would make any of the speakers I have in mind look like pikers. We have all heard it said, Mr. Speaker, by those who are anxious to destroy confidence in our parliamentary system of government, that there is no difference between the two old parties, that they only put on a sham battle at election time in order to divide the people, so that the successful party can carry on its programme of political patronage and political racketeering. That is the idea which a section of our press and some of our people are trying to instil into the minds of our citizens. Let me say at once that in any attempt to create such impressions as these, there is far more danger to our national unity and the future welfare of this country than those responsible for it imagine. When confidence is destroyed in our whole system of government, when a deliberate attempt is made to destroy confidence in the men and 'women who accept positions in public life and the responsibility that goes with it, the very foundations of democracy and of responsible government itself are undermined, and when that is accomplished we may well ask ourselves: Where do we go from here?
It is true, of course, that there are those in public life who do not conduct themselves in a manner which would warrant our confidence in them or confidence in the party or group with which they may be associated. That has been so in the past and in all probability will be so in the future. But that in itself places a direct responsibility on our citizens to be extremely careful whom they select to represent them in the administration of our public affairs. In my experience in this house during the past ten years I have found, generally speaking, that the members of all parties and groups are exceedingly anxious about and deeply concerned with the welfare of the people. It is true that we have our differences of opinion in regard to the best methods by which we can assist the people, but they are honest differences of opinion, not based on political expediency alone, as many would lead our citizens to believe. If we study the political history of this country I am sure we shall not come to the conclusion that those who have been our leaders in the past or are our leaders in the present are the kind of citizen who could be placed in the category of political racketeers. The very opposite is the truth. Those who have occupied the office of prime minister of this country qr that of premier of a province have all retired honourably from public life or have passed to their great reward with their praises on the lips of our citizens. Generally speaking they have endeavoured to give honest public service, and have been an inspiration to the young people of their day and generation.

But, sir, if a persistent effort is made to discredit everyone who accepts a position in public life, surely there can be no inspiration for our young people to fit themselves for the public tasks which someone must carry on.
I think a great deal of the criticism which is directed against governments arises out of the - fact that in all too many cases governments are expected to do the impossible, that they are expected to do things for the people which the people should do for themselves, and would be infinitely better off if they did. I remember after the close of the regular session of 1939 reading an article in the press which stated that parliament had prorogued without solving any of the problems with which it was confronted, but the article failed to point out that parliament had passed legislation dealing with those very problems. Such critics apparently fail to appreciate the fact that parliament is not an administrative body but a legislative body. While it is true that it is in parliament that laws are passed and policies enacted, it is equally true that those laws and policies are administered through departmental officials and other agencies. I know of no government which has solved all of its problems, nor do I know of any business concern which has solved all of its problems, or of any private individual who has solved all of his, for the very reason that new problems are continually arising. Governments have to face these new problems as they arise from time to time. The press feel free to criticize everyone who accepts public office, and that is right and proper, but even the press do not contend that they have solved all their own problems. As a matter of fact every decade since confederation has brought new problems for the press of this country to face, and some of these problems have made it exceedingly difficult for the press to carry on. But parliament does and can and always will deal with the problems that confront it from session to session.
There is another type of criticism to which I shall refer. I want it distinctly understood there is nothing personal in this, but it is a type of criticism which I think should not be encouraged. I am sure the house was shocked when one of its new members in his maiden speech made the statement that farmers never had received fair treatment from any government, and he gave as his reason for that statement that all governments had accepted campaign funds from the big interests, that they were bought body and soul before they ever started to function. This is a. serious indictment, one which involves not only the Bennett government and the present administration but previous governments whose

leaders have passed to their great reward- those of Sir Robert Borden, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir John A. Macdonald, and many others. It is a serious charge, and one wonders what evidence the hon. gentleman had on which to base such an indictment. One wonders, too, why anyone, particularly a farmer, should in season and out of season continue to support a party which he believes has never given the farmers a fair deal as a result of having been bought body and soul by the big interests.
No wonder that parliament as an institution is losing prestige and that respect for it is dwindling, when members will make such statements as these. The members making them have a conveniently short memory. We all remember how in 1911 Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government went down to defeat in an effort to improve the position of our farmers. At that time no one disputed that the so-called big interests were definitely opposed to Sir Wilfrid Laurier's policy of reciprocity. In our own counties of Huron and Perth there were five elected at that time, every one of whom was opposed to reciprocity, but I would resent the slightest insinuation that the people of those counties were bought or could be bought. As a matter of fact one of the things that has always made me feel proud to represent that constituency has been that its citizens cannot be stampeded in any way but think these things through for themselves, and then decide what is the best thing to do.
During the course of the campaign many catch-phrases were used, such as "No truck or trade with the Yankees". It was said that if reciprocity passed there would be two lines of rust running from the east to the west; and so on. These phrases and others of the kind did influence the people. I absolutely refuse to believe that the Canadian people or the Canadian government were "bought" on that or any other occasion.
In 1936, when the Canada-United States trade agreement was brought before this house for ratification, a lengthy and bitter debate took place. Every member of the official opposition opposed the agreement, but when the vote was taken it had the endorsation of the government, their supporters, and all the independents present. Will anyone suggest that the government, their supporters and the two independent groups in this house were bought body and soul when they voted as they did on that occasion? In 1939 we practically had a repetition of this vote. I remember well that one of those who vigorously opposed the passage of that agreement was the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). I
The Address-Mr. Golding
want to say that in my opinion there is no more honest and no more conscientious member in this house, and when he speaks for industry and the industrial worker he is speaking of something which is part of himself, because it has been part of his life's work. But, Mr. Speaker, nobody will make me believe that because he opposed those agreements the hon. gentleman was bought body and soul. This is a most unwarranted charge, one which could not be substantiated if a judicial investigation were held.
In the city of Toronto we have a financial sheet whose editors in my opinion have tried their utmost to discredit three outstanding veterans of the last great war, and so far as I know they are still carrying on in the same way. It is most unfortunate that when men and women are giving of their time and substance for the good of the country, the whole time of these people seems to be occupied in trying to discredit someone connected with the administration. About the only thing, it seems to me, they have to be thankful for as each day draws to a close is that another day has afforded them another opportunity to besmirch someone's reputation and standing. I am quite sure that if this government were bought body and soul by the big interests, opposition to them would not be coming from that particular source.
I have taken more time than I had intended to refer to these matters, but I feel very strongly about the prestige of parliament as an institution. I suggest to every hon. member that while we resent unfair criticism of the house and of its members, it lies within our own power to make this House of Commons a place which will have the respect and confidence of every one of its members and of every citizen of this country. I appeal to each and all to consider this his or her responsibility.
My advice to the government is to carry on efficiently and honestly, as they have been doing, the great task which has been assigned to them by the Canadian people.
There are many problems which, if time permitted, I should like to discuss, in connection with our farms, in the matter of taking boys off the farms, and as regards farm prices. But fortunately we have in the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) one who is a farmer in my own constituency, who is operating a farm and making a success of it, and I feel free to go to him and talk over'with him any of these problems. I do not think therefore, that I should take up the time of this house in stating the case for the farmers of my riding. Also the Minister of National
The Address-Mr. Golding

War Services (Mr. Tliorson) and I were desk-mates for four or five years. 14 seems to me, therefore, it would be time wasted, for me to discuss these matters in the house when I have access to these ministers in. the manner that I have.
I appreciate, too, the responsibility which rests on the official opposition. I believe that in general they are trying to carry out honestly and efficiently the duties which fall upon them in this critical time. The leader of the official opposition (Mr. Hanson) does occasionally hit below the belt, but I am not going to say anything more about that, and I know he won't expect me to say otherwise, because-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the blare of political trumpets, both in the house and across the country, sounding out praise and condemnation of the government's plan of a plebiscite, it seems that other matters of. importance have gone into the background. Perhaps if I were to give way to my immediate impulse, I would have something to say about this plebiscite business, but I think I shall wait until the bill comes down and, for the present, deal with another matter which I consider to be of vital importance at the present moment.
The matter I have in mind has so far not been dealt with in this house since the commencement of the war. I refer to the relationship between Canada and the United States in respect of that country's defence of its northern frontier state in- the war with Japan. I refer, of course, to the United States territory of Alaska, our next-door neighbour to the north.
The house is aware of the fact that some years ago the President of the United States appointed a commission to investigate the possibilities of constructing a highway connecting the Pacific northwest with Alaska. I do not suppose that the United States in its administration is any more free from politics than is Canada or any other country, and I must confess that from my reading I have come to the conclusion that a good deal of political pressure was brought to bear upon

that commission, appointed by the president in connection with its work. From my reading I have reason to believe that the work of the United States commission on this Pacific coast route to Alaska was complicated by political considerations. To say the least, it did not take into account any possibility of impending war with Japan. I am quite aware, of course, that the intention in the first place was to have a tourist highway connecting Alaska with the western states of Washington, Oregon and California. I know full well that the tom-ist idea was what all those who were interested in the matter were concerned about.
I should like to read the names of those who were appointed on the United States commission. Of course, this has nothing to do with us directly, though indirectly it has. The chairman of their commission was Congressman Warren G. Magnuson, of Seattle, Washington. There was also Doctor Ernest Gruening, director of division of territories of island possessions of the Department of the Interior at Washington. That was a good appointment. There was Donald McDonald, engineer, Alaskan Road Commission, Fairbanks, Alaska. Perhaps that was a good appointment. There was Mr. J. W. Carey, Public Works Administration, Portland, Oregon. I read these names only to show that the idea of the commission and its work was specifically to run this highway from Alaska to the western coast states of the United States.
Following that, a Canadian commission was appointed by the present government. This commission was appointed on December 22, 1938, pursuant, of course, to the United States action in appointing their commission. I should like to read the personnel of our Canadian commission. I think it is interesting. The chairman of that commission was the Hon. Charles Stewart, whose address is given as Ottawa, and there were Brigadier-General Thomas L. Tremblay of Quebec; J. M. Wardle, Department of Mines and Resources, Ottawa; Arthur Dixon, Department of Public Works, Victoria, and J. W. Spencer, whose address is given as Vancouver.
I am not going to criticize this severely, but I would point out that at any rate Mr. Spencer is secretary-treasurer, I believe, of the David Spencer Company of Vancouver and Victoria, one of the largest department store institutions on the Pacific coast. It goes without saying that these men are interested in having that highway go along the Pacific coast, through British Columbia, to the north, eventually reaching Alaska. Naturally, they are going to be interested from a business point of view, and perhaps no business benefits

The Address-Mr. Hansell
from the tourist trade more than does the department store business unless it is the oil and gas business.
I discover in my study of this whole matter that no consideration whatever was given to any other route to Alaska than the British Columbia route. In fact, certain representations were made to our Canadian commission from people in Alberta, but the commission refused a hearing. This is from the report of the commission:
Requests were also received for meetings at Edmonton and Fort MeMurray to enable the representatives of those places to present the views of their people as to the advantages of a route through Alberta to the Yukon and Alaska. The commission found it impractical to accede to these requests, the order in council creating the commission specifically confining its consideration to routes through British Columbia.
That commission was appointed in December, 1938. It did not begin its work until July, 1939; the war broke out in September, 1939, and the government here, in setting up this commission, gives them strict orders to confine their investigation to the one route in British Columbia. They could not consider any other route. The government must have been aware that there were other routes to Alaska which were just as accessible and through which it was just as easy to put a highway as any route in British Columbia; yet once again, such was the lack of foresight of the government, that the commission was impaired in its work.
There have been developments since then. I know, and I have already recognized, that what was in the minds of both the United States government and1 the government here was to have a tourist highway. But as late as May, 1941, Congressman Magnuson of the state of Washington, who was chairman of the United States commission, recommended the immediate construction of this highway from a military point of view. I read from a press dispatch from Washington dated May 23, 1941:
Immediate construction of a $25,000,000 highway from the United States through Canada to Alaska, approximately 1,600 miles, as a precaution against invasion from Siberia, was .recommended to State Secretary Hull Thursday by the Alaska international highway commission. The commission's report, made public by its chairman, representative Magnuson (Democrat, Washington), said that Russia, if so disposed, could attack from existing bases in Siberia.
From that dispatch you will see, Mr. Speaker, that the chairman of the commission must have realized that there was impending danger of a military nature in connection with that northern outpost of America; yet his commission studied only the British Columbia
route. What actually happened? General Marshall, United States army chief of staff, rejected the British Columbia route as being unsound from a military point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext: Where is that remark of General Marshall's found?

speechtext:
I saw that in a press clipping, which I might read. This is a dispatch from New York dated December 17, 1941, in which these words appear:
-General Marshall, army chief of staff, rejected the long-cherished dream of a highway to Alaska.
Of course that is just part of the dispatch. Mr. William Albee, who was considered a specialist on Alaska and the Yukon, and who was the author of the report of the Magnuson commission, was called before the federal planning board, and this is what he said, which, by the way, is from the same New York dispatch dated December 17, 1941:
The Alaska highway commission's work was complicated by political considerations and took no account of war conditions. . . . Its primary objective was to build a road linking the important coast towns of Alaska with the American west coast area. It developed into a Seattle-to-Juneau log-rolling junket.
Further on, he says, referring to a route east of the Rockies:
Our present estimate is that if the work of moving in the road-building equipment is begun before the end of January-
January is here now.
-there can be a road built to the Bering straits and military trucks rolling on it at express speed before the winter of 1942. With the Russians doing the same kind of work on their side of the Bering straits-and I was given to understand in Washington that this is an integral part of the project-we can carry out an encirclement move against the Japanese from positions in Japan's front yard, back yard and side yard instead of from thousands of miles away as at present.
That was before the outbreak of war between Japan and the United States. Just what are the immediate needs? This entire matter must not be regarded too lightly. With Japan entering the struggle and the United States compelled to take action, let us make no mistake about it; the north American continent is in danger. I think British Columbia is in danger. I am glad to see the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), who comes from Vancouver, in his seat. Perhaps he knows moire about this than any of us. I said British Columbia was in danger. The Yukon is in danger. Alaska is in danger; and while I am dealing with this point, I would remind hon. members that it
The Address-Mr. Hansell

would not take very much to isolate British Columbia completely from the rest of civilization.
I do not know if we altogether realize the position. Many hon. members come from Ontario and Quebec; indeed, from the point of view of membership, Ontario and Quebec control this parliament. But there are several great provinces out west. I wonder whether hon. members realize the situation. There are only two railways and one highway going into British Columbia. All that is necessary, whether it is done from the air or by sabotage, is to blow up a couple of bridges on those railways, or cave in one or two tunnels, and British Columbia is absolutely isolated from the rest of Canada. You would not be able to move a machine or a soldier to that province.
I do think-and I have had this in mind for some time-that this parliament should1 know exactly the situation that exists in British Columbia in relation to the entry of Japan into the war. I believe the Prime Minister [DOT] should meet with us in a secret session and tell us exactly the situation that exists in British Columbia. He should tell us exactly what defences we have there. He should tell us exactly the number of men we have there in the army and air force. He should tell us the number of planes and equipment we have there. He should confide in this parliament in connection with these matters. I am exercised about this thing; it is serious business. Not only are these territories in danger -British Columbia, the Yukon and Alaska- but, as Mr. Albee said or implied, as a piece of military strategy the cooperation of the three nations, the United States, Canada and Russia, in carrying out an encirclement move against Japan by means of a highway to Alaska, is most essential at this time.
I do not wish to suggest in one breath that certain political pressure was brought to bear upon the governments and commissions, and be interpreted as going a bit political myself in the next breath. If I wished, I could recommend that such a highway run through southern Alberta, because that is where my constituency is located.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It should be through Medicine Hat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Medicine Hat says it should run through there. All right, I'have no objection to that. If I liked, I could recommend that the highway run through my constituency and also through the rich Turner valley oil fields located therein. But I am not going to

suggest anything of the kind. It does not make any difference to me whether the highway comes through Coutts or Sweet Grass and through southern Alberta, or whether it comes through North Portal and thence through Saskatchewan or, if you wish, through Emerson and up through Manitoba. But I do say that such a highway must connect with the industrial areas of the United States, and must run north by way of Edmonton.
Perhaps one of the greatest authorities on the north and defence projects in northern territories, a man who has been called in to advise United States defence authorities, without question favours the route from Edmonton, north. I refer to that eminent arctic explorer, Doctor Vihjalmur Stefansson. What does Doctor Stefansson say? I read from an interview with him reported in the Philadelphia Record under date of May 20, 1941. It states in part:
Of the four routes to Alaska that have been proposed, any two could be built for less than half the cost of one battleship; the least difficult to construct could be built in half the time required to turn out a battleship. This latter inland highway, Doctor Stefanssen says, would reach Alaska via Edmonton, Alberta, and the Mackenzie river, and would be largely self-fueling, since it would skirt two extensive petroleum fields, the tar sands of the McMurray district of northern Alberta and the oil region of Fort Norman on the lower Mackenzie. . . . Impartial analysis of the four routes from the military defence point of view seems to indicate that, although one of the two coastal routes might be advisable for communication purposes if two roads are to be built, the inland route through Alberta -would be by far the most valuable in the event of war and would most certainly be the choice of army officials if only one highway were to be built.
The article goes on with further explanation, and I am told from authoritative sources that there is no reason why that highway could not be started now. There are tractors going through that north country every winter, hauling huge machinery of one kind and another, while the ground is still frozen.
I would recommend that a new commission be appointed immediately. The old commission is now defunct; it is dead; it has finished its work. I do not know how much it cost, but in the light of events which have since occurred, its work was absolutely worthless. As a matter of fact, the commission itself is not certain as to whether or not it should recommend a highway. May I read one part at the conclusion of its report. This is contained in a press release handed out after the report was submitted:
It agrees also with the opinion expressed by its engineering members that it is not practicable to offer a sound recommendation to the

The Address-Mr. Turner
government either as to the merits of any of the alternatives of the "A" route or the comparative value of the "A" route and the "B" route-
Both of which, by the way, are British Columbia routes.
-and it agreed with the recommendation that provision be made for further field work on the "A" route in the season of 1940, as outlined in the engineering reports.
In view of recent developments, there is no use in bothering with that commission now; there is no use even in thinking of putting a highway through British Columbia now. I would recommend, therefore, that a new commission be appointed immediately, that the members of such commission be entirely unprejudiced politically and from a business point of view. I would recommend, however, that the ministers of highways or their appointees in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and perhaps Manitoba, be on the commission, or appear in an advisory capacity. They know the machinery; they know the territory. Routes have been surveyed, and they are the men who can give information. I would urge that they be instructed to dispatch their business with the most careful thoroughness, but with the greatest haste. They should be instructed to see that the right machinery is moved in as soon as possible, while the ground is frozen, and that they seek to have the work done this year.
In the light of development in the Pacific, the importance of such a move cannot be stressed too forcibly. The danger is clear; no time should be lost. It is not sufficient to say that the United States fleet will protect the northern part of this continent. Since the wTar began, the unexpected has happened more than once. One of the greatest fleets in the world was outmanoeuvred in one of the most surprising pieces of naval strategy. I refer to the invasion of Norway. Let us not be asleep or fooled in this matter. Let not the governrrient blunder here. We have had our Hong Kong; we have had our Dunkirk. Let us be aware, and act now with respect to this highway to Alaska, lest we have our Norway on the north American continent.
