speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on what seems to be the topic of the day, namely conscription, and also something about the plebiscite which will come before our people shortly for their endorsation or rejection. I do not, however, believe I could do any better to illustrate my views than to say that after studying public opinion for some time very closely I have found that it would require considerable research to discover the origins
of what might be called the Toronto movement of uplift and control. There are probably traces of it right back to the days of muddy York. But it is within the last thirty years that it has really come into its own, attracting the attention of the outlying masses and drawing from them due and fitting comment and, at times, appropriate action. The full record of its activities must be left to the admiring historian, but in the short time at my disposal at least a note or two can perhaps be made.
It begins with 1935 when the best people, who are the life and soul of the movement, appeared on the streets and in the haunts which they frequent, wearing nice red, white and blue rosettes calling for national government. The laudable purpose for which national government was desired was to trim down the Canadian National railway by tearing up hundreds of miles of rails and to turn over what was left to the management of people of whom the movement approved. An unsympathetic public opinion failed lamentably to respond, and the great project failed.
But the dauntless spirit which inspires these drives did not long remain depressed. There followed, after a brief interval, the Leadership league. Surely this noble and inspiring experiment has not so soon been forgotten. This was directed towards creating in the outlying and dependent areas watchful committees which, under direction from the head office, would see to it that the elected representatives obeyed instructions-or else! In the latter event they would be replaced at the next election by more malleable material. How unfortunate it was that when an election occurred a little later, there was no Leadership league to exercise control and give direction, with the lamentable result that there were elected in large numbers members of whom the movement disapproves. But what had happened to the Leadership league? Why, it had died untimely of a combination of troubles-teeth-cutting, convulsions and infantile paralysis. Very sad, very unfortunate!
But again there was a rallying of the broken forces. This time it took the form of the Ontario voluntary constabulary association. Headed by one whose eagle eye can see treason and a disposition towards subversive action through any number of closed doors, it stripped for action with all the necessary accoutrements, uniforms, passwords, secret gatherings, training in manoeuvres. How it happened that despite the distinguished approval of the attorney general of Ontario, it wilted and died before it had a single scalp to its credit-not one person was landed in gaol-is a mystery, but this is indeed the melancholy fact. It only illustrates what a tough world this is for noble experiments.

2'he Address-Mr. Turner
But it is not altogether a record of failure. There are bright spots of achievement. Con-spicious among these was the performance of the hijacking commando in its surprise attack upon the Conservative committee of organization in Ottawa in November. In a movement of rapid action, which puts to shame recent tactical performances in other fields, they took the committee into captivity, put chains on it, and provided it with a leader who embodies all that the movement yearns for and demands. Some lads from the west who went to Ottawa to deal with the business that the meeting was called to consider, have been showing a most mutinous spirit, writing to the papers in protest and that sort of thing. But they might as well understand that if they want to stay with the grand old party, they must wear the yoke of submission. Toronto will supply the leader, make the policies and, if the miracle of victory happens, distribute the spoils on the basis of rewarding home virtues first.
The zeal, alertness and determination with which subversive ideas and tendencies are detected and trodden on has often been demonstrated, and this has never been more in evidence than right now. The approved missile in these cases is the manifesto. A memorial with the names of a few leading figures attached is considered to be a formidable weapon; though it must be sadly admitted ' that the results do not seem to bear this out. Within the last few days it has been found necessary to issue such a manifesto. Within twenty-four hours of the appearance in the Newr York Times of a dispatch indicating that Canada was taking a direct part in the proceedings of the allied war council, there was action on the Toronto front, showing how watchful and determined they are in resisting revolutionary change. Let Canada send her representations to London in the good old colonial style, and if London graciously approved, they might then go forward to the allied council. Thus said1 the manifesto; such was the demand of the alert watch-dogs. Good old blimps!
All these movements and activities, all these champions of "what Toronto says must be done" have now come together in a grand crescendo of demand, affirmation and denunciation by the device of the committee for total war. All their names are appended to the latest manifesto. Here are to be found the signatures of the National government leaders, the Leadership leaders, the voluntary constables who rallied to save Canadian civilza-tion, the wrecking brigade that stormed the Ottawa Conservative meeting, the alarmists

who issued the warning against Canada trying to act like a nation. Here they are pigging together, heads and points, in the same truckle-bed, as the eminent Mr. Burke would say. And with them, selected individuals from outside points who have joined in the great crusade.
The purpose of the great crusade is to do their thinking for the elected members of parliament, inform them as to their duties and instruct them in their performance when parliament meets. It is only necessary to see the two hundred names attached to the manifesto and to read its text, to realize that the Leadership league managed to leave a descendant.
It has to be recorded with pain that in calling in the outsiders, two slips were made. Two of the hand-picked membership turned out to be dissentient. One of these indicated an inclination to think that perhaps the members of parliament in intelligence and patriotism were the equals of their would-be instructors and could be relied upon to make their own decisions. But the gentleman who made these observations, only having served the country with distinction in both the Ontario legislature and the dominion parliament, and in the high office of attorney general of Ontario, was obviously not in the same class with the distinguished amateurs who had matters in hand. Moreover, he comes from Kingston, where the vice of independent thinking is still practised.
The other dissenting voice-that of a woman who had served at Ottawa in five parliaments -showed a similar lack of understanding of the technique of the movement. She actually had the crude idea that they ought to know who was putting up the money. Ought she not to know that this information is given only in camera? Clearly, it is a case of back to the wilds of Grey county for the lady-she is not yet acclimated to Toronto standards.
It is very regrettable that discordant voices should be raised not only in the gathering itself but outside in the waste spaces, in doubt, in derision and in repudiation. I have here, for instance, a newspaper which has the audacity to deny that the movement is the outcome of a spontaneous spasm of anguished patriotism-a low-down sheet that dares to say that the great rally "appears to have been just about as 'spontaneous' as the drafting of Mr. Meighen for the Conservative leadership." But this newspaper is published in Kingston and is under the blight of that town.
Meanwhile, the great movement is well under way with drums beating, flags flying and men shrieking. It has posh quarters in the

The Address-Mr. Turner
Royal York, which is a quite elegant hostelry. It is not thought there will be any trouble about the rent.
If I did not say another word and took my seat now, I think the whole story would be just about told of how a group of racketeers from a city named Toronto got together and I am informed by many people of Ontario that they have had that province in their hip pocket for some time and also have had the lead-off man in that province over a barrel so long that he has become warped. But that gang are not satisfied with that; they are aiming to get control of Canada itself. They are pounding away on the word "conscription" in order to rile up the people. They are using that method just as a means to gain their real objective, namely, the ousting of this government and the gaining of control at Ottawa. In all sincerity I question whether that group is as much interested in conscription as they are in gaining [DOT]ontrol. I might say that I am referring to the people in Toronto-I understand there are some good people there-and not to the members of the house. If the matter were brought out in the open from behind the bush, we would find that conscription is just camouflage, that the pay-off is control.
If ever we needed unity in Canada, we need it now. That was emphasized quite strongly by the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald.) But I shall have to be shown how we can have unity when one city is trying by every means possible to dominate and control the rest Of Canada and is continually belittling and torpedoeing our war efforts, which the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, Prime Minister of Great Britain, termed as magnificent.
Let us get right down to the marrow of this question regarding this countermovement organized by the so-called money manipulators. Why has this clique been continually out to get the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government? 'What is their real reason? It is simply that they know full well that they cannot bulldoze, stampede, railroad and muscle in on our present Prime Minister. That is what is burning them up. That is what is eating out their hearts. He is not a "yes" man. For once they cannot get their own way regardless of how much money they have or control. That is the real reason.
If there is one quality our Prime Minister has, it is that he is always cool, cautious and careful. To some he may seem to be a little slow at times, but it is just as well that he is that way. He has those qualities, and I am proud that he has them, particularly during a period of war or any other crisis.
Now, a few words about the plebiscite. I have always been taught that a promise made is a debt unpaid. On many occasions the Prime Minister has said that he would not enforce conscription unless he first consulted the people. I made the same promise on many occasions during the last election. The Prime Minister and the government are now seeking to carry out that pledge and are appealing to the very people themselves. Is that democracy? What is wrong with it? Time and time again we and others have condemned Hitler and Germany for breaking pledges, treaties and pacts, but when this government seek to carry out theirs, they are condemned.
Let us never forget that the people are the highest court in this dominion, and that they are our masters and we are their servants. Should that situation ever change, then the heart and soul of democracy is destroyed. I sincerely believe, Mr. Speaker, that holding a plebiscite is the honourable course for this government to take at this time, and I commend them for so doing.
Now I want to say, Mr. Speaker, what I think would take place in Canada if ever those sharks in Toronto got control here. About the first thing to happen would be the wiping out of the excess profits tax. Away would go the price-ceiling idea, and the sky would be the limit so far as profits on war equipment are concerned. On that very point let me say that maybe this is what that gang mean by "total war effort"'-get everything out of this war that it is possible to get, because the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, whom this group has forced in as leader, speaking on that very subject in the other chamber on December 6, 1940, is reported by the Senate Hansard of that date, page 62 of the Senate Debates, to have said:
I have no sympathy with those who would tax profits at 100 per cent. People will not work for nothing. Human nature is the same in war time as in peace, and instead of helping the war effort you are defeating it by stripping people of the stimulus to toil and run their business right. Leave the incentive, and make the reward greater the greater the toil and the greater the success. You have to do that. You do not do it under this bill. I do not exaggerate at all when I say that I have had business men by the dozen tell me that they are leaning on their oars; they have nothing to work for. They say: "We might just as well take it a little easier now, for we are only working for taxes anyway."
We are all familiar with the song, "Roll out the Barrel." You have heard it many times, Mr. Speaker. That would be played again if those gentlemen'got into power; only then it would be, "Roll out the pork barrel," instead of the beer barrel, and I should be -very much
The Address-Mr. Turner

surprised if under the control of Toronto our army would1 not soon resemble the Mexican army of a few years back when there were no privates and every soldier was a general or an officer. Those are only a few of the things which we might expect if the Toronto outfit should take control, but I am not afraid to trust the people of Canada to see that that shall never take place.
While I am on my feet, I want to pay a tribute to my district, which was well represented in the great battle for the defence of Hong Kong against overwhelming odds. Their stand in that battle will go down in history as equal to any made by gallant, courageous troops in any other war, past or present.
So much for the question of conscription and the plebiscite.
As food has been mentioned in the speech from the throne, I take this opportunitv to make a few observations with respect to wheat. I did not oppose the wheat policy of the government last year because I understood it was just a temporary policy, just trial legislation for one year only. But I must say to the government at this time, when we are all striving to preserve unity to the utmost in Canada, that we must, above all else, keep a proper economic balance right across the entire country, and I am sorry to say that that balance does not exist to-day. Due mainly to war contracts and government subsidies for plant extensions, and so forth, which I know are necessary, eastern Canada, particularly Ontario and Quebec, has the big end of it financially, and quite naturally they are having a great boom in business generally and are enjoying a period of prosperity. This is easily proven by a report in the Toronto Globe and Mail-there is Toronto again-of January 27, 1942, where I find this headline: "A surplus of $600,000 for Toronto." But, Mr. Speaker, what of the western provinces, those all-important wheat-growing areas? Almost the opposite is true. The farmers are striving and labouring to keep their heads above water, to keep going and stay off relief. That is what I refer to when I say that there is not a proper economic balance right across the country.
If we could weigh it on the scale, the indicator would show that the balance overwhelmingly favours the east. When a situation of that kind arises, it is up to the government immediately to take action. In addition to what I have already said, let me show how, by our action here in setting up a schedule of prices for labour on war projects, and so forth, and providing a minimum wage of forty-five cents an hour, plus cost 
of living bonus, which is little enough, we have automatically made it tougher for the farmer.
Here is the farmer's situation now as I see it. We first of all guarantee him seventy cents a bushel for his wheat, No. 1 northern, basis Fort William. That is not enough, particularly during war time. It will be noted that the price in the United States for May wheat is S1.30J at Chicago. We tell the farmer that he must sell his wheat only at the point of delivery stipulated in his permit. But we have done more than that. As I have just said, we have automatically raised the price of labour which the farmer must have, particularly during the all-important harvest season, to forty-five cents an hour. No farmer can pay forty-five cepts an hour for labour on seventy-cent wheat, plus bonuses, but less freight and dockage. Therefore we are clipping the poor farmer at both the top and the bottom. He is being pocketed by our own action. Let me give an illustration.
I was present at the beginning of the harvest season last year when an order came through for 1,600 men at $3 perhaps $3.50 a day, plus board, et cetera, and not one man of the hundreds present came forward. I personally spoke to many of those men, and their answer was that they wanted to get a job in a munitions factory at forty-five cents an hour. During the harvest period last fall I took a trip through part of my riding, and on one farm I saw a poor old lady, sixty-five years of age, on top of a grain stack, working away there when she should have been at home listening to the radio or at least doing some easier job. On another farm, on the next section, I saw a little girl twelve years of age driving the tractor, while her father operated the power binder behind. He told me that he had tried his best to get help, offering $4 a day, but had not been able to secure it. That little girl should have been out playing. I am sure she must have been tired at night.
I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and to the government that the farmer be given, say, $1 a bushel for No. 1 northern wheat, not at Fort William but at the point of delivery. If all the farmers of Canada are taxed equally and contribute equally to the treasury of Canada, why should they not withdraw from that same treasury share and share alike? No farmer should be penalized by the difference in freight rates just because he happens to farm a little farther away from Fort William than another farmer. Just as a further suggestion, the government might, if it so desires, consider paying that $1 a bushel on the first

The Address-Mr. Mclvor
1,000	or 2,000 bushels only, and then scale the price down from there. Such a plan would certainly take care of the thousands of the smaller wheat farmers all over western Canada.
I know the Minister of Agriculture had a job on his hands last year when we had such a large carryover of wheat, and with the new crop coming in, nevertheless I think we should simplify our national wheat policy and make it easier for the farmers and everybody to understand by considering cutting out the wheat acreage reduction plan, bonuses, et cetera; and tell the farmer what he is going to get in cash on the line, and let him store his wheat, if he wants to, on the farm and pay him for it. The machinery set up under the wheat acreage reduction plan is all that is necessary to take care of the inspection and so forth that would be required.
Therefore, in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the minister and to the government, and particularly to the Prime Minister, who represents a farming constituency in Saskatchewan, the province which produces the most wheat of any province in Canada, to give the poor farmers of western Canada the assistance necessary to keep up their very important end in our war effort and at the same time to bring about a better balance across the country generally, which in turn will create greater harmony and certainly a higher degree of unity in Canada from one end to the other.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when there is something on your mind the sooner you get it off, the better for yourself.
In opening my remarks I should like to congratulate not only the mover and the seconder of the address, but also the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), who I am sorry is not in his seat and the leaders of the other groups, who have been so constructive in their suggestions that one would almost think they were Liberal-Progressives.
To touch first upon what, to me, is the most important subject, I will say a word on the plebiscite. Neither in the last war nor in the present one have I felt that I could tell a young man that he should sign up, nor have I ever allowed my better half, as far as I could control her, to send a white feather to anybody. First, God gave that boy his life and to God he is responsible. As the old Book says, "the dust shall return to the earth as it was, and the spirit... .unto God who gave it"-not to the government. Second,
because if you put a soldier's uniform on a coward you cannot make him a soldier against his will, any more than you can put a gown on a profligate and make a saint out of him, or by painting a pump, change the water. I would add, as another reason, that it has been my sad duty on more than one occasion to break the painful news of a loved one missing or gone beyond. Just before I came to Ottawa I had to bring the news to a young wife, to the mother and father and family of one of the finest young men at the head of the lakes-where they are as good as any in Canada-a Christian young man and a first-class athlete, that he was missing, and when I saw the effect on the parents and the wife, I felt that I was not going to take the responsibility of telling anybody that he must enlist. But I was extremely proud that my own boy enlisted before he told me of his decision, and whether, when he goes into the air he comes safely down again, or his spirit soars up and beyond, is less to me than the consciousness that he is "white" all the way through. But it is my duty to support every young man who goes overseas in everything which will make him a soldier battling an accursed thing, and everything that the government can give those young soldiers it is our duty to give them. As I have said, if a boy is not a soldier at heart, if he hasn't "got it under his belt", you cannot make him a soldier. But I admit there are certain things that we must do. We must show the need. In our own way we must act whole-heartedly.
I should like to congratulate the government upon its choice of the new Minister of Labour, Mr. Mitchell. I worked with the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell and with the late Hon. Norman Rogers on the youth training scheme, which was one of the most constructive measures that a Canadian government ever put into effect. I know that from Fort William not hundreds but several thousands of young men have passed through that youth training and are now engaged in war work or overseas -on the land, in the air and on the sea. Mr. Mitchell himself was a worker. I believe that any man who is Minister of Labour should know how a man feels, like after a hard day's work. How can he best legislate for the toiler without some personal knowledge of the man's problems?
I admit I am biased in favour of labour. You can trust the workers through thick and thin; they are the cream of Canada, and, with labour willing to do its best, we as a government should give them the best possible leadership. In the interests of an all-out war
The Address-Mr. Mclvor

effort there should certainly be some equalization of wages and results. I know something of the difficulties which come to those whose task it is to handle men. I realize that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and! his fellow ministers have a terrific job. I would suggest that they throw out some inducement to men to. join the infantry, because to-day service in the air or in the navy holds superior attractions for many of our young men. If the pay of the foot soldier were increased from $1.30 to, say $1.50, it might facilitate recruiting in that arm of the service.
When I think of the war work of Canada I am not just sure whether we have enough men to supply all our various needs. Recently a farmer who had spent $10,000 in equipping a splendid herd told me that he was sending them to the butcher because he could not get help. Perhaps there are not enough men in the country for every phase of war work, but to my mind it is the duty of the government, and they should have a free hand, to ' say whether a man can serve better on the farm or in the machine shop or elsewhere.
Public opinion changes rapidly. The other day, when I saw that a United States army had landed in Ireland, I thought, "Boy, they are in for a fine time over there. Once they get a peek at the cruelty and the devastation which has been wrought in Belfast, that most beautiful city in the British empire, they will get a taste of the thing they need to open their eyes." And knowing something of Ireland and its characteristics, I think they may be taught the rudiments of how to take care of themselves and how to learn to fight and to beat the enemy.
As I have said, public opinion has changed quickly. In a letter from my brother, a member of the cloth, a real soldier and a real man, who is on the coast of Washington, he says that a little while ago public opinion there was anti-Churchill, anti-British, anti-Canada and anti-Roosevelt, but since Pearl Harbour was attacked they are going "all-out" in order to show that they are anti-Hitler and against everything that supports Hitler.
This change in public opinion reminds me of my own attitude towards Russia. I have been guilty of reading everything that I could get hold of about Russia. Some of it was true; some of it was not, but my attitude towards that country and its people, and towards communism as well, has changed. To be called a "red" to-day is no disgrace. Some time ago I visited Tim Buck. I did so because he had

been through a bad wreck. I did so as a minister; for, if I had not, I would have been like the priest and the Levite who looked and went by, fearing lest public' opinion might criticize. I know what I had to meet during the dominion election because of that action. I. was called a communist. But my constituency knew me perfectly well, far better than my critics, and they voted accordingly. I would advise the government to have reexamined all those who are interned as opposing our war effort. I think they should be given an opportunity of getting into our war work, because, as I understand the government, it is not their desire to keep men in prison but rather to give them an opportunity of doing their best.
Canada is doing a great job. Among those engaged in our war effort is the former leader of the opposition. When I think of former members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party and of the Conservative party contributing to our war effort-and this includes the Hon. Dr. Manion, who was chosen to lead his party at an all-Canadian convention-I cannot help believing that the best brains of Canada to-day are engaged in this country's war effort. I suggest, therefore, that we have in reality a better national government than we could otherwise hope to have.
When a man wishes to serve, I think it is wise that he should be given an opportunity to serve in that capacity which he is best fitted to fill. It is not fair to put him to serve where he is not best fitted to serve. Take a trainee who has signed with the air force; he has spent years fitting himself for service in that force; he wants to fly. Well, you hurt that man if you do not give him an opportunity to fly. Another man wishes to join the navy, let us say, and he, too, is a trainee. He should be allowed to serve in that capacity, because he will make a good sailor and he will not make as good a soldier; he will not be a soldier of the same calibre as a sailor, if he were allowed to go to sea. I think, again, of the premiers of our provinces who are willing to go all-out in their own way, whether we think they are right or wrong, in supporting the government, and in this regard I would make a suggestion. I think there are some things the provincial governments can do to help the war effort.
It may surprise you, Mr. Speaker, to know that I made my rounds of the beer parlours of the city of Ottawa. I was not surprised that I did not find a member of this house in any of them, either man or woman, but I did find these places crowded, and I think the premier

The Address-Mr. Green
of this province would do well to try to settle his own affairs and not leave it to the dominion government, because that traffic does coarsen life and unfit soldiers, muddling the brains of men.
Another thing is this. The provinces should do something with regard to old age pensioners. The sum of $20 a month is not very much to-day. Pensioners need a bonus; so do soldiers' wives and soldiers' widows. In my opinion the provincial governments could very well exert themselves and go all-out in their own way.
I notice that in most of the countries at war there is a seven-day week, twenty-four hours a day, in the production of war materials. Well, I have been taught from my youth that the human body needs one day in seven, and if a man does not take one day in seven he will certainly take all his Sundays in a row. I might mention our own car works in Fort William. Girls have gone in there to work with strong healthy bodies and vigorous minds, and I have known of several instances in which they were compelled to retire from their jobs for a month or two on account of ill health. If you do not take your Sabbath day you will pay for it. I would remind hon. members of the old proverb, drawn from the Bible, that if you break the moral law, the moral law will break you. We must "remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." A man who toils six days a week needs a day off in which he can get something spiritual to help him in his work. The greatest leaders in every age have recognized the need of one day's rest in seven, and I am sure the Minister of National Defence agrees with me in this regard. After a man has worked for six days, he needs the seventh day to rest. Of course, what he does on the Sabbath makes all the difference in the world. If he rests, in order to build up his mind and his spiritual powers, he will be the better fitted for the work he has to do. If he does not, so much the worse for him.
A famous physician, Sir James Crichton-Browne, said:
We doctors in the treatment of nervous diseases, are now constantly compelled to prescribe periods of rest. Some periods are, I think, only Sundays in arrears.
The eminent conductor, Sir Landon Ronald, discontinued his Sunday concerts in 1928 on account of his health, saying: "I can no longer work seven days a week."
Gladstone attributed his long life to his rigid observance of the Lord's day.
President Coolidge was asked: "Cannot I worship God in the green fields?" He replied: "You can, but you don't."
Of course, I believe that the place of prayer is the place for a man to spend part of his Sunday, because he will hear something there that will put him in communion with the Master Workman, who will give him that stimulus necessary to fit him to play 'his part in life's work.

Mr. Speaker, when one has been in this house for a time, one can sense the feeling, the atmosphere that prevails in this chamber. I am convinced, and I think you will agree with me, that at this session there is a tenseness, an earnestness and a depth of feeling which I hope and believe goes even deeper than partisan feeling in the minds of members of this house. And I hope this feeling will be allowed free rein by the ministry, because if that is done, decisions may be reached, right here in parliament, which will point the way for the Canadian people during this dark, yet challenging period in our national life. Therefore, believing the house to be in such a frame of mind, may I state quite frankly at the beginning of my remarks that to-night my aim is to point out to my fellow members, and through them to the country, that Canada, our nation, of which we are justly so proud, is in deadly peril. I repeat those words; Canada is in deadly peril; and I aim also to convince members of this house and the people throughout the country that certain things can, should and must be done.
I speak as a representative from Canada on the Pacific. Canada is a two-ocean nation. I am always intrigued by that verse which is carved over the main door of this building, and which is as follows:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
On the east we have those old provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec, forming Canada on the Atlantic. But on the west coast, constituting Canada on the Pacific, we have only my own native province of British [DOT] Columbia.
Since the house met last November, war has come to the Pacific. The fires of war are raging round that great ocean. War is the grim business of killing and being killed. Those of us who served in the last war are
The Address-Mr. Green

only too well aware of that fact. But this war is far more grim than the last one by reason of the development of the bombing aeroplane, which has made possible the slaughter of thousands upon thousands of civilians, men, women and children, and because the war in which we are engaged is a war of extermination. Nowhere will it be fought with more savagery than on the Pacific. That was made perfectly clear on December 7 last, when Japan struck at Pearl Harbour while her envoys were still negotiating with the envoys of the nation she attacked. Japan struck and crippled the United States fleet. Crippled the United States fleet! Those are ominous words for Canadians on the Pacific, because year in and year out we have been told that our defence on the Pacific was the United States fleet, and that, in fact, was the truth.
In the seven weeks that have intervened, the British fleet in the Pacific has also been crippled by the loss of those two great battleships, the Prince of Wales and the Repulse. Various strategic islands have been seized. Hong Kong has been taken, wiping out our courageous but ill-fated, ill-equipped and ill-trained Canadian sacrifice force. Hong Kong! Members of this house and all Canadians must burn that name into their memory, for we have a score to settle with the Japanese over Hong Kong. And it must be settled not in North America but on the far side of the Pacific.
These seven weeks have seen Manila taken and the Americans fighting a last-ditch stand for the Philippines; Malaya overrun, with the British fighting a last-ditch stand for Singapore; and Singapore, whether it stands or falls, no longer effective as a great naval base. Bases have been taken in Borneo and in the Celebes for an attack on Java, which is the heart of the Netherlands East Indies. Bases have been taken in the Australian islands, as a prelude, the Australian people believe for an attack on their mainland. May I point out to hon. members that Canadians on the Pacific have great sympathy for Australia. We have a keen understanding of their attitude, because we realize that Canada may eventually be placed in exactly the same position.
In short, these seven weeks of war on the Pacific have placed Japan in control of that ocean. As my authority for that statement, I quote none other than the Britist Prime Minister, Right Hon. Winston Churchill, who, in his speech on January 27, only this week, is quoted as having said:
For a time, therefore, naval superiority in the Pacific and the Malayan archipelago passed into the hands of Japan. How long it will remain in Japanese hands is a matter on which

I do not intend to speculate, but it will be long enough for Japan to inflict many heavy and painful losses on all the united nations who have possessions in the far east.
Further on in his speech, referring to the United States as well as Great Britain, he said:
I expect -and I have made no secret of it that we shall both receive severe ill usage at Japanese hands in 1942.
So Canadians on the Pacific find themselves closer to war than any other Canadians, and more directly involved. I do not wish to make light of the peril in which our fellow Canadians on the Atlantic find themselves. They too are in great peril, but on the Pacific ocean there is no island fortress of Great Britain between Canada and the enemy. There is as our only protection a crippled United States fleet. There is an enemy-not without a fleet, as the German Reich, but an enemy with a first-class navy; an enemy with a first-class and very strong merchant marine, an excellent air force, and an army that has had experience in warfare for the last ten years. And there is an ocean-the Pacific ocean, such a vast ocean that there is plenty of room for fleets to operate without their being discovered.
Canadians on the Pacific coast have already experienced that sudden warning which can be appreciated only by those who have heard it in their homes. They have heard coming suddenly over their radios-"An enemy attack on the Canadian coast is imminent"-and then the radio station shuts off. The attack, presumably, was expected from aircraft carriers off the coast. Sooner or later that attack will come. It did not come at the time we received the warning, but I am convinced that sooner or later it will come, and our coastal cities and hamlets will be bombed. The people of British Columbia are not whining about that. They are not of the type who whine, any more than are any other Canadians. We are not a whining nation.
They realize, too, that the United States has bases in Alaska. To the north and northwest of us there are great United States bases which afford considerable protection to us, but at the same time those bases are a great menace to Japan. The base on the Aleutian islands is, I believe, the nearest hostile base to the shores of Japan. Therefore those Alaskan bases may be-"may be" I repeat- the next in line for attack by Japan. It may be that included in the objectives of such an attack would be our own city of Prince Rupert, the Queen Charlotte islands, and even Port Alberni. These may be sought by the Japanese as nuisance bases, or even as invasion bases.

The Address-Mr. Green
Should they be taken by the Japanese, it would be possible from them for the enemy to bomb our coastal cities at short range; they would be in a position to bomb our shipyards, our war industries. The greatest shipbuilding industry in Canada is on the Pacific coast. Our heaviest merchant-shipbuilding programme is being carried out on that coast. It would be possible to bomb United States coastal cities where, again, are naval bases and great aeroplane plants. I believe 90 per cent of United States aeroplane factories are located on the Pacific coast. It would be possible to make the whole of British Columbia a battle-ground, and even to bomb the prairie cities such as Edmonton and Calgary.
This is not just an idle fancy of my own. I should like to read to hon. members dispatches from Japan published on January 9 of this year, only about two or three weeks ago. I quote this report of an article in the Japan Times and Advertiser, controlled by the Japanese foreign office:
The Japan Times and Advertiser, controlled by the foreign office, declared to-day it was within the realm of probability "that the armed forces of this country will land on the American continent" . . . "The contention that the United States cannot be invaded" the article declared "is as much a myth as that the Maginot line could not be taken or that Singapore and Pearl Harbour are impregnable. .	.	. The fall of both the Philippines and
Singapore was forecast soon. After that, the newspaper went on, "It will be for us to say when, where and how we will strike."
Let us not forget that the shortest route from Japan to San Francisco is by the Aleutian islands and the coast of British Columbia- much shorter than by way of the Hawaiian islands. Let us remember that Vancouver is closer to Yokohama than is Sydney, Australia.
Canadians on the Pacific coast know, also, that the Canadian armed forces on that coast are hopelessly inadequate to deal with an attempted invasion. They know that large numbers of our troops on that coast are home-defence troops, called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. This means that fighting troops from Prince Rupert could not go, as a unit, to the neighbouring panhandle of Alaska, should Alaska be attacked. Fighting troops from units defending Victoria at this time could not go to neighbouring San Juan island, or across the strait of Juan de Fuca to Port Angeles. It means that the fighting troops guarding the city of Vancouver could not go across the line to Bellingham, should Bellingham be attacked, because many of them are home-defence troops. Our units could not go across to aid United States troops -joint defence council or no joint defence
council. On the other hand, if you please, young Americans could and doubtless would be sent to help us, should we be attacked.
That is an intolerable position. It is intolerable for a brave and proud people. It is intolerable for a nation which in the last war sent out fighting men who proved themselves on the battle-field the peers of any men on this globe, a nation which in this war has sent abroad young men of the same breed.
Canadians on the Pacific coast know, too, that what forces we have are not all adequately equipped. For example, we find this press dispatch on the front page of the Vancouver Province of January 3, nearly a month after Japan had declared war:
Guns coming here within few weeks.
The dispatch goes on to say:
A number of anti-aircraft guns have been allotted to the Vancouver defence area, and on their arrival here within the next few weeks will be mounted at strategic points through the district, an army spokesman announced to-day.
And as for rifles for the reserve army- some of them have no rifles at all. Those who have, I believe, are, or were within the last few days, using old United States rifles with red bands round the top, signifying that they were not fit to be fired.

speechtext:
There are men in the active army on the coast who have no rifles at all. These are not men in the battalions, but in other branches of the active army. Every soldier on that coast should have a rifle and should be trained to use it. He should be trained to fight regardless of what branch of the service he happens to belong to. And again, Japanese fishermen on the Pacific coast have been made to turn over their boats. I think this was a wise move on the part of the government, but Canadians out there see these Japanese fishermen who naturally may be embittered, going back to their villages up and down the coast. There are eighteen hundred of these fishermen, and if they saw fit they could guide enemy naval forces to every bay, every landing place and perhaps every gun on the Canadian coast. Meanwhile the government ponders what is to be done next. And they see that this government has done everything possible to foist the responsibility for air raid precautions upon the provinces and the municipalities, although it is clearly a problem of defence and should be handled by the dominion.
To sum up, the Canadians on the Pacific coast are restless; they are worried, they are annoyed. Now they are given a plebiscite in which the following question is asked:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
What will go through their minds when they are voting on that question if there happen
[Mr. Green.J
to be air raids threatened at the time? The Prime Minister talks of unity, but this plebiscite will not create unity among the people on the Pacific coast. So much for the peril in which Canada finds herself.
I shall now go on to suggest certain things which can, which should and which must be done. First of all, let us cast out from our minds at once the thought: It cannot happen here. That has been the curse of democratic countries in this war. Let us replace it with the thought: It can happen here; right here in Ottawa, in Halifax, in Toronto, in Vancouver, or in any other part of Canada. No thought will make us more realistic, no thought will help us more to avoid reverses and to gain victories.
For example, I am convinced that the ministry have not given serious consideration to the possibility of a Japanese invasion of Canada. If they had, they would not risk the delay and confusion that will be caused by this plebiscite. I am convinced further that the staff on the Pacific coast and the staff here in Ottawa have not considered what they would do in the event of invasion. Our new chief of staff is reported in the Vancouver press of December 18, less than two weeks after Japan had declared war, as follows:
"Canada's Pacific coast defences are, I believe, capable of coping with any probable attacks that we may have to face", Lieutenant-General Kenneth Stuart, chief of the Canadian general staff, said this morning on his arrival here following a three-day inspection of defence areas on Vancouver island.
"I have no doubt," General Stuart added, "that I will be accused of complacency in this regard, and yet that is far from correct. We are fully aware of the dangers that have developed with Japan's entry into the war and we are adjusting our forces to meet these dangers."
The chief of staff stressed the possibility of hit-and-run attacks along the British Columbia coast. " I do not say we can prevent these attacks but I do think we are in a position to deal with them."
Further on, the report states:
The possibility of a Japanese invasion here, he believed, is extremely remote.
That reminds me of the words of Air Marshal Sir Robert Brooke-Popham, who said in Singapore on December 8, the day after Japan struck:
We are confident. Our defences are strong and our weapons are efficient. We bad plenty of warning and our preparations are made and tested.
Words which unfortunately held more of hope than of fact.

The Address-Mr. Green
If this invasion attack should come, probably our generals would make another of these strategic retreats with the remnants of our forces to the mountains, leaving the people on the coast to their fate, and in the result thousands of Canadians would have to die to get back what need never have been lost. Let us make up our minds now; let us tell our commanders and our people that not one inch of Canadian soil is to be yielded without a fight.
My second suggestion as to what should be done is that we should give our commanders armies that can fight anywhere. At the present time we arc giving commanders in Canada units made up of two kinds of soldiers, those who can be taken beyond Canada and those who cannot. That makes it impossible to build up here an efficient fighting force. Let us go further and make certain that we can keep these armies reinforced with fully trained troops, not troops who have had less than sixteen weeks training. I believe at the present time, and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) can correct me if I am wrong, that even the fourth and sixth divisions arc not up to full strength.

My suggestion is that we make certain that there are ample reinforcements, and that means conscription. Why should we dodge this issue of conscription as a means of organizing our man-power? I was greatly impressed by the report of a Gallup poll taken in Great Britain where the common
people of Great Britain were asked what advice they would give to the common people of the United States about the war. One of these suggestions was that man and woman power should be organized efficiently and at once, that they should not take half-way measures. Why should we in Canada hesitate? In Great Britain we had Prime Minister Churchill saying these words this week:
It looks as if we were in for a very bad time. But, provided we all stand together and provided we throw in the last spasm of our strength, it also looks more than it ever did before as if we were going to win.
Canada should throw in more of her strength and not leave it all to Great Britain. This government, I believe, feels much the same; otherwise it would not be calling for a plebiscite. Let us have conscription, and let us have it without delay, but let us make it complete conscription of all our resources right down the line, including industrial and financial resources, as advocated, for example, by the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League.
My third suggestion is that things must be done now, without delay. We should pay more attention to timing. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he spoke on Monday, gave us a little curtain-lecture on the importance of timing. Well, the principal thing about timing in this war is not to be too late. Let us realize that in this war every day is precious. Japan struck nearly two months ago, and this government rushed in to be the first to declare war. Apparently it is going to be the last to rush in to take up the fight. The ministry should have moved at once to put this nation on an all-out war basis. But they did not. Now, although they see the need, they are taking time out to hold a plebiscite, which means, at the minimum, a delay of three months. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is making a mockery of talk of a total war effort. We must wage war now-not a matter of months hence.
Finally, I have suggestions with respect to the Pacific front.	The Pacific coast is a
front, and should be treated as such. It is a war front, and on that Pacific front we should have one supreme commander. I believe that we now have three commanders-and the ministers will correct me if I am wrong. I believe (hat the army commander, the navy commander and the air force commander work together by cooperation rather than any one of them being in command over the other two. That was the situation at Pearl Harbour, except that instead of three commanders there were only two. But Canada,
The Address-Mr. Green

itlmost two months after Pearl Harbour, still has a triple command on that Pacific front. Also let us make it a fighting command where we shall put, not one of our older generals, but one of our most aggressive commanders with experience overseas in this war, and with a fighting staff built up on the same basis as those in Great Britain. We may see fighting on the Pacific coast before our troops in Great Britain get into action.
Then let us build up a striking force, not a force that will merely sit there to defend, but build up on the Pacific coast a striking force which could be an expeditionary force. For example, why should Canada not have air troops; trained and in position on that coast? They would be of the greatest advantage in recapturing any point of the coast that might be attacked and captured. No troops would be of more use, but apparently we have none in Canada at the present time. I suggest that the government obviously is treating the Pacific coast as. a secondary theatre of war. The Prime Minister said the other day that perhaps-perhaps-there was nothing certain about it-we would raise another new division to help defend Canada after the fourth division had gone to Britain. Again, yesterday, when I asked him whether Canada was to be represented on the new Pacific defence council, he said he did not know anything about it at all, that it had only to do with the far, far away southern Pacific, and apparently he was not very much interested.

There has been talk of that, for months, ever since Japan struck, but no plan, so far as I am aware, has been announced. There is another grave danger on the Pacific coast. Canadians on the Pacific are entitled to and insist on getting complete protection from treachery, protection from being stabbed in the back. The rest of Canada, under successive dominion governments, failed to listen to our representatives from British Columbia when they asked for an end to Japanese immigration. But now what British Columbia members for the last thirty-five years have been telling other members of the house would happen has come to pass, and the rest of Canada must do its part. It must now come to our help. I appeal to private members on the government side of the house to see that the ministry do come to our help in this matter. We have at least 24,000 of Japanese origin in our province, all in the coastal area

fishermen, men working in our woods in the lumbering industry, men farming on both sides of the great Eraser river valley, which means that they are astride both of our transcontinental lines. There has been treachery elsewhere from Japanese in this war, and we have no reason to hope that there will be none in British Columbia. If we were in a similar position, if we were Canadians in Japan, we might feel much the same; we would be only too willing to assist British troops should they attempt to land on the Japanese coast. The only complete protection we can have from this danger is to remove the Japanese population from the province. I believe that the commanders of the fighting forces on the coast and the special committee on the Japanese problem set up by this government have advised that at least all Japanese

The Address-Mr. Cruickshanh
males be removed from the coastal areas. The ministers will correct me if I am wrong. This government announced on January 14 that it would define certain areas as protected areas and move out from those areas Japanese nationals-not saying whether they would move out the Japanese born in our province or those who have become naturalized, and no man can get a fishing licence without taking out naturalization papers. But it has not yet been done, and British Columbia is waiting, waiting rather impatiently, to know whether this was just a stall, to know just what this government intends to do and when it intends to do it.

In conclusion, the situation as I have stated it is as I see it and, I believe, as it is seen by the great majority of the Canadians on the Pacific. I am in deadly earnest because I believe that this nation is in dire peril, and also because I believe that at this time, as never before, the members of this parliament hold in their hands the future of the Canadian people. In this dark and challenging time Canadians look to us here in the Canadian parliament. Let us rise to the occasion and give them the bold and far-seeing leadership to which they are so justly entitled. .

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this house, are extremely fortunate to-night to have the privilege of hearing, not just one, but two members from British Columbia. I realize that some hon. members from the rest of Canada have long awaited this privilege; I have been looking forward to it myself. I did not know that I was to have the good fortune to follow the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green)-a good personal friend of mine, though we may disagree politically.
I want, for a few minutes, to discuss the war effort, particularly in so far as it concerns the conscription issue; the Japanese situation, of which I have heard a little during the last few minutes; and agriculture.
In days gone by, all of us used to hear of the famous "Four Hundred". Coming from a farm, I never had the privilege of living among them, but I have read a little about them in the Toronto Globe and Mail or some such paper. More recent interest is in the famous "Two Hundred". Most of the "Four Hundred," I have understood, wear diamonds; they are invited to the houses of the Vanderbilts and similar mansions. Now, having heard of the famous "Four Hundred", I wanted also to discover what I could of the "Two Hundred". One of the good things that the Dominion of Canada does is to provide a library in which one can get information concerning all the leading-lights of Canada and the world at large. I repaired to the library to get some information. I recommend to hon. members, or some of them, that they spend a little of their time enlarging their information, as I do. In the library there is a shelf of biographies of the great men of Canada, and of history, and I want to commend the librarian, whoever he may be, whether appointed by the last government or the present one, for his discerning talent in selecting books. The first book I found on the shelf was a life of Winston Churchill by Robert Sencourt. Nobody can find fault with that selection; Mr. Churchill is one of the greatest men that ever lived, one of the outstanding figures of this or any other generation. Then I found "Roosevelt, A Study in Fortune and Power". Can anybody name a man who has contributed more to the allied cause than Roosevelt? And no man has done more for the British empire in cementing the friendship between Roosevelt and Churchill than has Mackenzie King.
Naturally, being a modest and unassuming young man from the far west, I hesitate to tell you of the next book I found in the library on the shelf of lives of famous men. I hope that my hon. friend the member for Vancouver South is listening carefully. I will mention, first, the name of the author, Blanchard Jerrold. It is a little red book, well bound; its title, standing as the book does on that shelf of lives of famous men, is "George Cruikshank". Any hon. member may get this book, and I shall be happy to autograph a copy.
I shall not take up much time, on such a serious occasion as the present in congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne,

The Address-Mr. Cruickshank
although I claim that I may have a greater knowledge of such speeches than many hon. members who are sitting in this present session. If the Speaker would permit me- I do not know whether I would be in order or not-I could divert now and give half of my speech in the Japanese language; let me say that if conditions in the west are allowed to continue as they have been going, everybody in British Columbia will, in a few years, be speaking Japanese.
I am very proud to say that my roommate is now serving overseas, and I have the privilege of looking after his riding as well as my own. I say I consider it a privilege, because he is where a good many men ought to be who are talking about conscription. Just this evening, while the hon. member for Vancouver South was speaking, I received a cable, which I will read to the house because it concerns two hon. members from British Columbia who are supporters of the present government, and I have full authority to speak on their behalf in this connection.
Mr. George Cruickshank, M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Met Alan Chambers in town and heard Churchill in parliament yesterday. Advise you join the army and come over.
James Sinclair, M.P.
I want to say to this committee of Two Hundred, "Join the army and go over; don't try to send others over."
As I said, I have heard something in connection with speeches made in the house by those who move and second addresses in reply to speeches from the throne. My roommate made his speech so often in my hearing that, before he was through, I could have repeated it in English, French, Japanese and Esperanto and done it better than he did, so far as being word perfect is concerned. One word which I heard frequently in that speech and which possibly some of my friends in the party to which I belong do not like particularly, was used by him with regard to the war effort of Canada-the word "complacency". He chose that word, and it echoed and re-echoed from one end of Canada to the other.
Let me assure the house in all seriousness that I support a great deal of what the hon. member for Vancouver South has said with reference to the Japanese situation in British Columbia. Let me make this statement, in fairness to myself and to those whom I represent-and I may say that I represent with the hon. member for New Westminster, 75 per cent of the Japanese population in British Columbia. We are not satisfied, and under our democratic system we have a right

to say so in the houses of parliament. We are not satisfied with the action that has so far been taken in my riding, at least, with regard to the Japanese situation.
I would rather enjoy it if any member of this house or anyone else were to question my patriotism or loyalty; but much as I love my country, I love my family more. I live in the Fraser valley where we are surrounded by Japanese. I have read all about Pearl Harbour, and I can tell the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) what our views are out in that part of the country. I want to tell him emphatically what we think, and I say this with all respect to him; for with only one exception, so far as this House of Commons is concerned, that exception being the Prime Minister of this dominion (Mr. Mackenzie King), I revere the Minister of National Defence more than any one else. I say to him, however-and I am speaking my own opinion as a member from British Columbia, and one who should know something about the Japanese situation-that he has been ill-advised with respect to the situation in our province.
We cannot afford to wait; we cannot afford to take chances after Pearl Harbour. I wish to make my position clear, and it is my duty to do so. I was never consulted by the so-called committee-not the Department of National Defence, but the so-called committee, who know nothing about the Japanese situation in that province; nor was any other member from that province consulted. I regret the mistakes that have been made in that connection, and I have expressed my views on every platform on which ff have spoken. I am not, however, worrying about mistakes made in the past so long as they are not repeated in the future. I want to warn the house and the Minister of National Defence-and I do so in all sincerity, irrespective of party-that there are no people living at present in the city of Ottawa who have any greater or more intimate or more thorough knowledge of the Japanese situation than is possessed by the members elected to parliament from that part of the country in which is to be found the "Japanese peril."
Let me pass on now to the subject of agriculture. I like to talk about that subject, because the only people who, I understand, have made any money in agriculture in the last few years are some of the farmers in Ontario. One of my hon. friends-I could call him by name, but I am not permitted to do so, and I have forgotten his riding-has a couple of race horses. I am ignorant about race horses; the only one I ever bet on came in last. I do

The Address-Mr. Cruickshank
not know anything about that sort of farming, but I do know something about agriculture, British Columbia agriculture at least. It is true that we are not getting a better price for our agricultural products than we did get; it would be foolish to deny this. But I should like to refer hon. members to the Vancouver Daily Province, a representative British Columbia paper. On the day I left British Columbia, that journal carried fourteen advertisements under the caption "milker wanted", in each of which the pay was stated to be $55 to $05 a month and board.
I realize that many members of the house cannot know a great deal about farming. That is natural. As I say, however, there were fourteen advertisements for "milker wanted", paying from $55 to $65 a month. To digress for a moment, I may say that for the first time since I have been in Ottawa I approve of one of these officials that have been appointed. I refer to Mr. Gordon, a man who knows his business and is administering the price-fixing plans. He has the courage of his convictions, and it is only men of that type who should have such responsibilities.
When we were getting a certain price for milk we were paying from $20 to $25 a month for labour, and now we are paying $55 to $65 and board and cannot get labour. I want to keep my record clear on this question. I do not blame labour; it is not getting what it is entitled to. But labour will agree with me, I believe, when I say that the prices which were set, so far as agriculture is concerned, were not set on the same basis as in the case of labour. So far as labour is concerned, they were set in accordance with high prices; this was not so with regard to agriculture.
Let me point out to my hon. friends to the extreme left, for whom I have great admiration, that the greatest safeguard labour has in Canada, or in any other country for that matter-I hope the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) is present-is organized agriculture. That is the greatest safeguard that labour can fall back upon. You could not keep a union going to-morrow if you did not have agriculture to fall back upon, and it is in the interests of labour as much as it is in mine to see that agriculture gets a fair break. As my respected leader said, agriculture is as much an integral part of the war effort as tanks, guns, or anything else. Everyone, I believe, agrees with that; but you cannot carry on a true war effort until such time as you put agriculture on a sound basis. I repeat, you cannot establish a true war effort until you put agriculture on a parity with labour and industry, and no one can tell me that this has yet been done.
Let me quote a few head-lines from the Ottawa Citizen:
Controlled price for butter urged by dairy farmers.
Here is another:
Proper proportion of guns and butter held victory aid.
As you will see, I am leading up to conscription.
Here is one point to which I think the government should pay particular attention. I strongly disapprove of the policy of bonuses. I am not from Saskatchewan or Alberta or Manitoba or any of the desolate countries, and I strongly disapprove of the policy of bonuses. I want to quote a head-line that appeared in a prominent paper last night, and to repeat something I said in the first speech I made in this house. The greatest asset Canada wifi have to offer when we come to discuss peace terms is our vast store of food. I do not think we should curtail the production of wheat; I think we should encourage it. I would far rather see more wheat grown in Canada than more gold produced in Kirkland Lake, British Columbia or anywhere else. This is the head-line that appeared in last evening's Citizen:
Bread Selling in Athens for $15 per Loaf.
Famine conditions in Greece are so acute that two thousand persons died in Athens alone in a single day, and bread sells for $15 a loaf, the Journal de Geneve reported to-day.
I need not read the rest of the dispatch; but is it not reasonable to expect that food will have more to do with the peace terms, after this war is over, than guns, tanks or anything else? I am firmly of that opinion, and I believe it is nonsense to curtail the production of foodstuffs. I think the government should pay the prairie farmer an adequate return on a reasonable acreage for as much wheat as he can produce, and let him produce it.
Tor a moment I want to turn to conscription. You may call it a plebiscite or anything you like, but that is what it amounts to. I honestly consider myself a friend of every man and woman in this house; at least I should like to think I am. I do not claim that I am more patriotic than any other hon. member. I do not claim that the party to which I belong is any more patriotic than any other party. I think we are all sincere in what we do, and so I hope what I have to say in this regard will be taken in good part, because I do not wish to give offence to anyone. In this, however, I speak as a veteran of the last war, as a farmer and as a member of parliament. For good and sufficient reasons
The Address-Mr. Cruickshank

many men were unable to serve in the last war; they were physically unfit, or something else prevented them from serving. But I must say-and in doing so I speak as a member of the Canadian Legion, and as a veteran accept full responsibility for what I am saying-that I think it ill-timed and ill-advised for any man to advocate, preach or talk conscription of the other fellow if he himself is under the age of sixty, if he did not serve in the last war, and has no son serving in this war. I am expressing my opinion, whether or not some people like it. I think it ill-advised for any man who is physically fit, of military age and not in uniform, to advocate that his neighbour's son be taken for this war. That is my opinion, and I stand by it. A great many of the men who have been talking about conscription know nothing about it. In the last war I served all the way from a private to a company commander; and I will take one volunteer in preference to any ten conscripts in any war. During my election campaign I said I believed, and I still firmly believe, that from the start we should have had compulsory selective service. It is the fairest way. But I want to repeat what I also said during the campaign, that it must be accompanied by the compulsory service of wealth and industry. That is what I said on every platform; that is what I still believe, and I speak as a returned soldier who is not afraid to go back to his riding at any time and face his electors. I believe in compulsory selective service from start to finish, but I believe that it must be accompanied by the conscription of wealth and industry.
I do not believe in red herrings, Mr. Speaker. I do not know7 where I heard it, but somewhere I heard that in some districts they can their lobsters and sell them, while in other districts they elect them. I am prepared to support any party that will come out with a legitimate proposition to help in winning this war; but when it is brought out as a red herring, as was the case with this famous committee of Two Hundred from Toronto, representing financial and vested interests, that is another matter. I will not say I am ashamed, but I am surprised that my good friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, whom I greatly admire, should even associate themselves with an amendment that will further such a dastardly attack on the democratic rights of the people of Canada.

speechtext: But we have not.
