speechtext:
Thank you; I
am glad to hear that. I for one stand by my pledge, and will continue to stand by it. That pledge was given also by my leader and even by Doctor Manion, who said that before conscription for overseas service would be introduced, the people would be consulted. I am asking my friends in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation to remember that. This government is doing the only honourable thing in asking to be relieved of the pledges it gave in good faith. You may question whether or not the pledges should have been given, but they were given. So I am asking my friends in the extreme left comer-not too extreme; half-way down- to get out and work for this plebiscite, as I intend to do, and to vote for it, as I intend to do. As a member supporting the government, I firmly believe that if we break our pledges, we lose all we are fighting for. Then, after we have been released of our pledge let my friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation ask me to vote with them for the conscription of wealth, industry and man-power.
It has been said of the Liberal party that we would not take other people into the government. I do not know how much time I have left, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps you could check up and let me have a few more minutes anyway.
I want to point out that we as a Liberal party have been criticized because we did not form a national government. That is all this committee-of-two-hundred smoke-screen is, with respect to national government. That is all Tory stuff. They think it should be a national government of a few mining interests, a few financial interests; that is all this smokescreen of conscription is about. They have not the courage to come out, as did the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and declare their stand. They are hiding behind the smoke-screen of conscription, and yet they ask us to bring in members of all parties, or members from outside the government, and persons outside the House of Commons.
Yesterday I listened to the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), and I heard his objections with respect to the new Minister of Labour and the new Minister of Justice who are to be brought from outside the House of Commons. But it will be remembered that during the last two sessions hon. members in my hon. friend's party were demanding that we bring in the best brains of the country from without the house, or from anywhere. We all know that; they demanded it.

The Address-Mr. Cruickshank
Vie now bring them in-and what do they do? They say, "Oh, you did not take them from your own little house around you." I may get around in time; maybe I should be over there on the government benches. But they blamed us when we did not take them from within, and when we have not taken them from without. What do they want us to do?
I want to say here and now that I have the greatest respect for the Conservative party, but I have not the slightest respect for the Tory party. Yes, I have great respect for the Conservative party. To be frank, I would not be here to-day if I had not had some friends in the Conservative and Cooperative Commonwealth Federation groups. I am willing to admit that. But I must point out that the Conservative party, when they asked us to form a national government did not have a man to offer. I would naturally assume that when they asked that, they wanted us to take a Conservative into the cabinet, but they frankly admit they had not one to give us. Yes, they admitted that they had not one to offer us, and they cannot deny it. I defy one of them to rise in his place and deny it. They had not one to offer us, I repeat, for the simple reason that they could not even get a leader among themselves. They had to go outside the party to get one. So, how could they give us one? '
I want to tell hon. members-and I defy contradiction-that not a solitary Conservative western member voted voluntarily for Arthur Meighen to lead the party. He was not elected. I have had disputes with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), but I respect him. He is the leader of a great party, and he is a sincere man who was elected by the popular vote in his riding. He was chosen by the vote of his members to lead his party. But the new leader was not elected at all; he was appointed by George McCullagh, and a few others. We cannot get a member to come into this cabinet; and if we cannot get a prominent Conservative among the forty or so elected representatives in the House of Commons- and how so many people made that mistake in Canada, I cannot say-I want to ask: Where will we get a Conservative to come into this so-called national government, governed and directed by the Financial Post of Toronto and a man named McCullagh? Where would we get them? We cannot get a prominent Conservative across the Dominion of Canada to come in, because if he has not been elected, he is a dollar-a-year-man, or a prominent official in the Department of National Defence.
Where are we going to get him, I would like to know-and I hope the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is in his seat.
I still have confidence in the youth of Canada. I believe I have made myself clear on the matter of conscription; even the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation will agree that I have made myself clear. It is my opinion that we can get sufficient volunteers at the present time. If the time ever comes-and it may-when we have to enforce conscription, then, party or no party, it must be done. I am a Canadian and a Britisher first; party comes last, so far as I am concerned.
I do not believe it is necessary yet to enforce conscription, but I must point out that if voluntary enlistments have not been what they should have been, nothing is more to blame than the Department of National Defence. At the time of the last war we had what was known as the intelligence branch. In this war, in so far as my private opinion is concerned, we have what is sometimes called the recruiting branch. I call it the stupidity branch," and that is the reason we have not more volunteers.
I should like to describe one case in the principal city of my constituency. This has reference to a young chap who earned a gold medal in his senior matriculation year at high school. He had the leading record in British Columbia, so far as graduation is concerned. This boy went to a Royal Canadian Air Force recruiting ofiice. I must add, in passing and I say this in all sincerity-that he was a Tory, I am sorry to say. I should have preferred him to be a Social Crediter, or something else. However, he was a Tory. Remember, I am not drawing on my imagination, because I could give the boy's name. He went to the recruiting officer appointed by the Department of National Defence-I am sure he must have been an officer appointed to keep them out. Do you know what he said? Well, he said, first of all, "Where are you from"? and the boy replied that he was from the farm. Well, God help the day when any son from a farm in Canada is not as worthy of consideration and respect as any other man -even if he may come from the city of Toronto. This recruiting officer said to the young man, "Oh, you do not want to join the Royal Canadian Air Force; you would not be at home in the officers' mess; look at your hands." That boy had earned his way through high school, even to the point of winning the gold medal, and yet he was told that he would not feel at home, because his

The Address-Mr. Cruickshank

hands were rough. But that boy bombed Germany on several occasions, and after a raid over Berlin he is now missing.
There is great stupidity in the recruiting offices, and that is the reason why we have not more volunteers. Then, there is another constituency I happen to represent, during the absence of my roommate. I refer to the constituency of Vancouver North. The second largest shipyard in Canada is in that constituency, and it is operated by a man having millions of dollars. That man has three sons, two of whom are twins nineteen years of age. The other is twenty-one years old. This boy is missing somewhere over Germany. The other two boys are serving to-day in England in the Royal Air Force. Some stupid, ignorant representative of this select outfit-God knows who selected it-called up the mother of this lad who is missing. The father of this boy is quite a wealthy man and has been doing a marvellous job in his war work. This stupid, ignorant appointee of some official who has undermined the government and undermined the war effort called up this lady and said, "I am sorry to tell you, but you have not a God's chance of ever seeing your son again." Why did he want to tell her that? These are the stupid asses who are to be found in that building not far from here. If you are short of recruits, I could get enough to fill ten divisions from the Jackson building, the national defence building or the dollar-a-day men.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) will excuse me if I do not try to follow the many arguments he has presented to-night. There is, however, one thing I must say. The speech you are going to hear now will not be half as good as the one you have just heard. Following two hon. members from British Columbia, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), and the hon. member for Fraser Valley, I cannot help realizing, as I am sure all other hon. members do, the grave situation that exists on the western coast. I would, however, point out to these hon. members that we in eastern Canada have realized for the last two years that the situation was very serious. Perhaps it is the newness of the situation on the western coast that has impressed the hon. members so emphatically during the last fewr weeks or months.	[DOT]
I agree that the western coast is in danger and that eveiy effort should be made to meet that danger. I am aware also that we have been in danger on the eastern coast for over two years and are still in grave danger. This

simply emphasizes the fact that Canada is a great and large country, and I am sure that Canadians, whether they come from the east, from the middle or from the west, are interested in one thing only-the defence of Canada as a whole.
Any remarks which I make this evening will of necessity be. quite brief. I have heard only a little of this debate because I have been here but a few hours since the session opened, having had other duties to perform during my short stay in Ottawa. I understand the mover, (Mr. Fournier, Hull) and the seconder, (Mr. Macdonald, Brantford City), of the address made eloquent speeches. It is just what I would expect from both of those hon. gentlemen because I have been with them in the house for the past six years, and I know they are able debaters. As to the substance of their remarks, there is naturally a great difference of opinion. From what I have heard I do not think I can agree with the substance of the remarks of either one of them.
I was surprised at the attitude taken by the hon. member for Brantford City. Brantford is one of the most patriotic cities in the dominion, and I do not believe his remarks represent the opinion of the people in that splendid city.
We have heard a great deal about the promises that were made in the election of 1940, and this will be the chief topic of my remarks this evening. I believe both the senior parties made a great mistake by stating as planks in their platforms that they were not in favour of conscription. If we had been honest with the people of Canada, as we should have been when a war was on, we would have told them that if conscription were necessary, we would be in favour of it. We find ourselves in our present position because we neglected to do that. In the light of present events it would have been both an honourable and a proper attitude for these two parties to take. Being wrong, then I contend that we only perpetuate the wrong by calling for a plebiscite. Two wrongs have never made a right, and I do not think any argument that can be presented now will make them right.
I saw a report of some remarks made the other day in Montreal by the premier of Quebec. He was addressing a mass meeting, and there was a clamorous cry against conscription. Young men who should be in khaki were clamouring against conscription to defend the_ country in which they live. The argument used by the premier of Quebec was that we should consider the position in which Australia finds herself to-day because she sent so many of her men out of the

The Address-Mr. Brooks
country. A good many of those men were volunteers. The fact that a man volunteers for active service does not mean that he will be sent out of the country; it is up to the Department of National Defence to say whether he shall be sent out of the country. If he is needed in Canada, hfe remains here; if he is needed overseas, he is sent overseas. To say that because we have conscription all our men will be sent out of the country and will not be here to defend the country if needed, is not a logical argument. It is one which should not have been used before an intelligent audience by the premier of Quebec.
I agree with the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White), who spoke yesterday and said that there was an implied promise on the part of the government. Som'etimes an implied promise is stronger than a spoken one, and in this case there is no doubt which is the stronger. It is a more binding promise than anything that could be said in the heat of an election. Then there was a definite promise by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-all hon. members heard it-to the effect that we must wage a total war. What does total war mean? I would say it means that we must wage war to the limit of our resources, both material and man-power. I believe that is the definition which the Prime Minister himself would give.
The Prime Minister says that he wishes to keep a promise which he made in the heat of the election to the people of the Dominion of Canada. He went on to say that the condition in which the world finds itself today is due to broken promises. That is just one of the reasons, and, I would say, the least. The present-day condition of the world is not due entirely to broken promises. It is due to the fact that the democratic countries of the world ignored those broken promises of Germany and Italy. They knew that the enemy countries were arming but they made no effort to arm themselves or prepare in any way to meet the terrible crisis which is now upon us.
I am opposed to this plebiscite being held, and I have four reasons for opposing it. First, I think it is unnecessary and unfair. Second, I think the money being expended! for this purpose should be used for other purposes where it wouldi do more good. True, it may be only a matter of $3,000,000 or $4,000,000, but every dollar counts at the present time, and there is no reason why we should waste one dollar or three million dollars. Third, it is a waste of valuable time. If the Prime Minister intends to bring in compulsory service for overseas-I think it is fair to
assume that he does because otherwise, why hold the plebiscite?-why should we waste three precious months? Now is the time to act, and time is very valuable to men who are being trained for our armed forces. Two or three months may make all the difference in the world, and on that count I say it is not fair or just that we hold a plebiscite at this time. My fourth reason is that to hold a plebiscite is shelving responsibility. We, the elected representatives of the people of this Dominion of Canada, if we have the intelligence we should have, are the ones who should decide this question, and here in this house is the place where the decision should be made.
Why do I say that this plebiscite is unnecessary? The reason is that I believe the people of this dominion would be behind the [DOT] government if they declared that compulsory service overseas was necessary. We need only look at the press of this country from one end to the other. I believe that the press reflects the opinion of the people and that the people of this dominion to-day would be behind the government in imposing compulsory service on this country if it were necessary. Furthermore, the government knows the actual circumstances, and the people do not. We in this House of Commons do not altogether know the whole situation. But the government hear reports every day from every sector in which the war is being waged and know the facts. Let them tell the facts to this House of Commons, and then place the responsibility on the elected representatives of the people to decide what shall be done.
I have said, Mr. Speaker, that a plebiscite is unfair. Why? Whom are we asking to decide this question? We are asking the mothers with sons of military age who would have to go overseas, mothers who do not know the actual facts. It is they whom we are asking to go to the polls to put their ballots tremblingly in the box to send their own sons away, and without knowing whether it is necessary or not. On that count I say a plebiscite is not fair. The same applies to the fathers of these young men, and to the sons themselves. But these young men, I believe, would willingly go if the great necessity for men for active service were pointed out to them.
As to recruiting, I am proud to say that I have good results in my own province of New Brunswick. About eighty per cent of the men who served under me have enlisted for active service. That is not true of every other section of this dominion. I do not know the facts, of course, relative to all the other

The Address-Mr. Brooks
sections, but I do know that there are sections which have done wonderfully well, and other sections which have failed miserably so far as enlistments are concerned. I have had young men say to me, "If they want us and we are needed, why does the government not enact legislation to that effect?" After the thirty-day training period the young men of this country were compelled to go into the service for the duration of the war and I can say without fear of contradiction that very few of these young men, who were told they had to stay in the service for the duration, complained. I could count on my fingers the young men who went through my training camp and complained of having to stay in the service after taking the thirty days or four months training. Nearly all of them accepted the situation as a necessity, and I believe that if the government had told them that it was necessary for them to serve not only in Canada but in any other part of the world where th'eir services were needed, they would just as gladly have accepted that fact as they did the other form of compulsion.
I have also had young men come to me and say that they were willing to enlist if they could first go home and consult their parents. I have had them come back to me after discussing the matter with their parents and tell me that they were sorry but they had to change their minds. These young men were humiliated and ashamed. But had their parents known that it was necessary for them to serve, these young men would have been spared that humiliation, and I am sure the parents would not have felt very badly about it either.
As I said a few moments ago, we are proud of our record in recruiting in the little province of New Brunswick. We have more than filled our quota on every occasion. That is also true of other sections. The little province of Prince Edward Island has a record of which it may justly be proud. I think most men have enlisted from a spirit of patriotism. I am quite satisfied of that. And may I point out to hon. members that in New Brunswick we have a mixed population? We have in the north our Acadians, of whom we are justly proud, and then we have in the south the descendants of the Loyalists, the Scotch, the Irish and the English. All these races in New Brunswick have been doing and are doing their share. The Acadians from the north have come to my camp in large numbers, splendid young men, as have men from every other section of the province.
There is another reason why possibly we have had more enlistments in my province, and this is not such a creditable one. We

have not the war industries in New Brunswick that are to be found in other parts of Canada.
I shall not take the time of the house to go into that to any extent, but I should like to give the following facts which were obtained in a study prepared for the Dalhousie University Bulletin on Public Affairs for the year 1940.
On a per capita basis, Munitions and Supply contracts to the end of 1940 amounted to $63 per person for Canada as a whole, but only to $19 for the maritimes. Conditions have changed somewhat for the better since then. Again, on the basis of $1,000 invested in industry, the figures show $205 for the dominion as a whole and $112 for the maritimes.
Government grants to industry for capital equipment have gone 42 per cent to Ontario, 41 per cent to Quebec, 10 per cent to the prairies, 4 per cent to British Columbia since then that figure for British Columbia has greatly improved'-and the remaining 3 per cent went to the maritimes, Nova Scotia getting 2.75 per cent, leaving New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island practically neglected. That may be another reason why the young men of our province have enlisted in larger numbers than men in other sections of Canada.
My own constituency of Royal has done well. Most of our farmers are dairymen and they find it very difficult to carry on at the present time on acount of the great number of young men, trained dairymen, who have left that part of the province.
Another great plea that was made by the Prime Minister was for national unity. It is hard for me to understand the conception of national unity in this dominion. I have not defined it for myself, and I do not propose to Undertake to do so for others, but I would ask this question. Is it unity when many of our young men from one section of this dominion go and fight the battles of Canada and very few men come forward from some other section? I do not think that sort of thing tends towards unity. I do not think that is the sort of thing we may expect to find in a united country. I might also ask is it unity for all the sons to go from one particular family-and I know of families where practically all their young men have enlisted- and to have other families with four or five sons not one of whom has volunteered? That sort of thing does not tend towards unity in a community nor, when multiplied to a great extent, does it tend towards unity throughout the nation. Will it make for unity in Canada when this war is over, for thousands of our men who have fought overseas to return and

The Address-Mr. Brooks
meet the thousands of young men who were on home service and home defence? There will be a barrier raised between those two
groups, and I foresee much discord and disunity so far as the young men of this country are concerned.
We talk of equality of sacrifice. I have mentioned the young men from New Brunswick serving in the army, alongside, of course, men from other parts of the dominion, and getting their $1.30 a day. But one can go through towns and cities and see thousands of young men, after working hours, parading the streets in their best clothes. Those young men are working in the factories and getting $5 to $6 a day. I contend that it is unfair that young men from one section of the dominion have to fight Canada's battles for $1.30 a day, while thousands of others, taking no such risk, are receiving four times as much for working in factories. Such conditions do not make for unity. It may be asked, what can be done about it? Well, we might arrange, if there are no industries which can be established in the smaller and outlying districts of the dominion, to take the men to the industries. Bring the men from New Brunswick to Quebec and Ontario; they would foe willing and glad to help in industrial work; and let Quebec, Ontario and other provinces supply their due proportion so far as service for overseas is concerned.
We -have heard Abraham Lincoln quoted in this house during the present debate. I happened to see not long ago a statement regarding conditions during the civil war in the United States from 1861 to 1865. This question of compulsory service is not new; it is as old as history. The issue has been fought in parliaments for a great many years in many countries. Lincoln, in .the United States, had his own troubles. At the time to which I refer, in 1863, they had the voluntary system, and it was not working well. The war which broke out in 1861 had so far resulted in an almost unbroken string of victories for the Confederate army. Early in the war the southern armies had pushed within thirty miles of Washington. The Union army was in a chaotic condition. Generals quarrelled; armies fought like undisciplined mobs; there was every indication that the Union would fail. Up to that time the Union had depended upon the voluntary system. In some states the militia would not even go outside the boundaries of their own state, and men were called up for service for only six months. As I have said, the situation was chaotic. Lincoln, in speaking
about the voluntary system at that time used these words; whether they are appropriate to conditions at this time is for us to judge:
Voluntarism is the unprincipled dodge of cowardly politicians. It has ground up the choicest seed corn of the nation. It has consumed the young, the generous, the patriotic, the intelligent and the brave. It has wasted the best moral, social and political elements of the republic, and left the cowards, the shirkers and the money-makers to stay at home and propagate their kind.
That statement, I say, may be worthy of consideration by the members of this house.
A few weeks ago we had the honour of listening in this chamber to the Abraham Lincoln of the present day. I believe hon. members all know to whom I refer. We heard Mr. Churchill say at that time:
If anybody likes to play rough we can play rough too. Hitler and his nazi gang have sown the wind; let them reap the whirlwind. Neither the length of the struggle nor any form of severity which it may assume shall make us weary or shall make us quit. . . .
Of "the broader world which lies beyond," he said:
We have to win that world for our children. We have to win it by our sacrifices.
He did not tell us then that it would be easy. He is not telling his people to-day that the road is easy. What is happening in England? What happened in England to-day? When Churchill came before the British House of Commons for a vote of confidence, the vote stood 464 to 1-practically unanimous. Why? Because Churchill makes and leads public opinion in that country. It was a magnificent tribute to a great leader and a great statesman, a man who tells his people what is needed and sees that those needs are carried out, as far as is possible for him to do so. He offers no apologies or excuses. He said to them, "I make no promises". I commend that to the people of this dominion and to the members of this house. We make too many promises. If we had not made promises which we could not fulfil, we would not have been in the position in which we are to-day. A wise man is Mr. Churchill. He makes no promises, and he holds no plebiscite in his country during war time to find out whether he should be relieved of those promises to satisfy new conditions. He told us, as I said a moment ago, that the road was not an easy one. He assured us it would be hard. He told us also:
We cannot for a moment afford to relax. On the contrary, we must drive ourselves forward with unrelenting zeal. In this strange, terrible world war there is a place for everyone, man and woman, old and young, hale and halt. Service in a thousand forms is open.

The Address-Mr. Brooks
And he reminded us:
There is no room now for the dilettante, for the .weakling, for the shirker or the sluggard.
Man-power is needed in this country. We have no less an authority for that statement than the adjutant-general in the Department of National Defence. He told us not long ago, and I believe what he said is correct, that man-power is the only power which will defeat Hitler. Let us, then, not be shirkers. If manpower is needed, if it is needed now, let us of this House of Commons not shirk our responsibility. Let us stand up and vote for conscription if it is necessary, and not throw the responsibility upon women and men and boys of this country who do not know the facts. I ask hon. members that when the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) comes before this house, they give it their full support.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are dark days for Canada and for our empire. The history of this war so far has been such as to create gloom, yet also to arouse many people from apathy and cause them to search and question among themselves, what is it that is wrong? To-day Singapore is in imminent danger. It is one of the last barriers in the far east; if it falls, Australia and New Zealand will be in grave peril. I hope that a message has gone forward to the people of the sister dominions telling them that while Canadians still live, they will never permit the heel of nazism or the Japanese tyranny to reign over those parts of
o.ur empire.
It is my intention to use the time allotted to me to deal with an element of total war which, in my opinion, has been sadly neglected by those who are directing our effort. I speak of morale. In any effort the first requirement is vision. It appears to me that those responsible for Canada's total war effort have lacked sufficient vision to see the importance of morale. It is too essential an element in total war to be disregarded. Apparently they do not understand that ideals and ideas are of the importance that they are and that, if we are. to succeed, they go along with the tanks and troops. Hitler's highly organized forces were led on by brutal ideals and perverted ideas; but, brutal and perverted as they are, they led a desperate people forward: in the factory, in the troops and on the farms. In Russia to-day the people are fighting for their homes and their lives, for an economic system in which they believe, a system for the people of Russia. Those people in Russia have gained economic democracy; they have yet to gain political democracy. To those people no sacrifice is too great. They will burn down

their homes and their crops; they will destroy their dams and their industries in those areas where they might fall into the hands of their enemies. It is the morale of those people which is saving the democratic way of life to-day, and has been saving it for months. The Russian front news is the most hopeful that we have had during the past dark days from any part of the war front.
In Canada we have a form of political democracy, but we yet have to gain economic democracy. We in Canada do not need' to be told what we are fighting against; what we do want to know is what kind of life we are fighting for. "V" for victory! Yes, but victory for what kind of life and what kind of reorganized Canada? We hear people in all parts of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, saying, "Well, things will be different after the war." I am sure every hon. member here has heard that. Then let us get a vision of what things will be like after the war. Of course,
I know there are some who say that we have not time for that now. But we must have time for it. We must give our people some hope of a vision for the future. That is what is necessary in order to get our people, as they do in Russia, to go out for total war. What they want to see in Canada is action which will give equality of sacrifice, if such a thing is possible in Canada to-day.
The vision that this government should give is a vision of a better life. When that vision and that morale are supplied, Canadians' contributions will be doubled. If that vision had been given by this government for the past two years, there would be no need for a plebiscite. No one suggests, in talking about a reorganized Canada, that we are going to ask the boys who crawled out of box-cars and out of the jungles and who went into the forces, to get back into those box-cars and jungles when the war is over. No one suggests that the million people or more who were on relief in 1938 and 1939 are going to be sent back on relief when this battle is won.
What is this government telling the people of Canada? What assurance is it giving those boys who have come out of the box-cars as to what is going to happen in Canada? This government has shown itself fearful of great ideals and new ideas. It is apparently afraid to present the people with a vision, which it should have done long ago. The spirit of Canada is great, but this government should give a vision which will arouse that spirit. The men and women who came to this country in the early days travelled in their carts and wagons and faced fearlessly and boldly the difficulties of forest fires in the east and prairie fires and blizzards in the west. In that way

The Address-Mr. Castleden
a great nation was developed. These elements were fought, and the people suffered and worked and planned-why? Because they had a future. They had a vision of bright things to come. That is what is needed- to-day.
Our people throughout the country feel today that they are being driven down a blind alley in darkness instead of being led out with a clear light ahead of them shining on a reorganized and reconstructed Canada worthy of the sacrifices that are being demanded and are being made. Morale is needed in every phase of our war effort: in our army, navy and air force; by the workers in our factories, in our mines and on our farms. Why this murmuring from agriculture? Mr. Speaker, the back-bone of any nation is the great mass of common workers and toilers, the people in the factories and on the farms, the people in the lumber camps and in the mines, the fishermen on the sea, the toilers who produce goods and wealth. These are the back-bone and being of any nation; and when the nation fails these men who supply the troops in time of war, it is failing the men who take the steel. The nation which forgets and neglects these people is failing deeply and inwardly. It failed them in time of peace, and it is failing them in time of war.
According to the statement given by the department, 260,000 men of Canada have offered on the altar of national sacrifice their lives, their blood, everything they hold dear. I want to know whether one thousand industries have volunteered even to lend their factories for the duration of the war. We do not ask that these factories be completely destroyed, but can any sacrifice equal that of a mother who gives her son? Why on earth cannot one big industry; why cannot all the industries of Canada, place their buildings, organization, managerial ability on the selfsame altar of sacrifice on which 260,000 men of Canada have offered to place their lives and everything they have? We are not forgetting that industry in this country refused to touch contracts even when a profit of 5 per cent was offered to them. Canadian industry is turning out great quantities of materials these days at its own price. There is unfortunately too much evidence to show that too many people in this dominion look upon war as a harvest time, the time when they feel they are legitimately entitled to amass great wealth and property for themselves. With their usual callous inhumanity and disregard for moral obligations, they fail to see that the harvest they are reaping is a crop grown on soil which is fertilized with the blood of their fellow men.

speechtext:
Any coupon-clipper who to-day reaps profits out of this war; those who demanded their profits in time of national crisis. They endanger everything that is worth while in our domocratic way of life. With everything we have we oppose such an outlook and such a philosophy as dangerous in a time like this. We are opposing that philosophy in the constituency of York South to-day. Perhaps the attitude of industry can be no better revealed than in a speech made on December 6, 1940, by the new leader of the Conservative party, speaking in another place. I quote what was said by Right Hon. Mr. Meighen, speaking on the War Exchange Conservation Act, as reported at page 62 of the Senate debates:
I have no sympathy for those who would tax profits at one hundred per cent. People will not work for nothing. Human nature is the same in war time as in peace, and instead of helping the war effort you are defeating it by stripping people of the stimulus to toi-l and run their business right. Leave the incentive, and make the reward greater the greater the toil and the greater the success. You have to do that. You do not do it under this bill. I do not exaggerate at all when I say that I have had business men by the dozen tell me that they are leaning on their oars; they have nothing to work for.
A lot of work they do!
They say: "We might just as well take it a little easier now, for we are only working for taxes anyway." You will get that result in any ease if you take away all incentive to work. But leave the incentive and let it grow as profits increase, and increase taxes as profits increase. There is no other way I know of to get results.

speechtext:
It is a sad commentary on the national life of this country that in the hour of need, business men by the dozen should be resting on their oars, with our men at Hong Kong needing equipment that was not there. Have we Quislings among the industrialists of Canada? Then the Toronto Daily Star of yesterday, January 28, quotes Right Hon. Mr. Meighen as having said :
If we have to conscript wealth to win the war we will, but people of common sense don't advocate that until the last gasp.
The Address-Mr. Castleden

This man is particularly anxious to conscript the man-power of this nation now, but he says that wealth must be conscripted only as a last resort. Blood should go now; wealth only at the last! In effect he says, "People, give your sons that we may keep our gold." May the people of York South do a service to the common mass of the people of Canada by sending here a representative who will work and strive along with those who say-and I quote from our amendment-"place the war industries, accumulated wealth and the financial institutions of Canada at the same time and on the same basis of sacrifice as the suggested extension of conscription of manpower."
That is the policy the people of Canada want, and this adiminstration ought to know it. I do not think a plebiscite is necessary; but if this administration is anxious to know what the people from one end of Canada to the other want, I challenge it to place upon the plebiscite a question in the terms of the amendment to the amendment : "Do you want industry, the war industries, the accumulated wealth and the financial institutions of Canada placed at the same time and on the same basis of sacrifice as the suggested extension of conscription of man-power?" This administration has passed more orders in council in less time, with parliament sitting, than any other government in the history of Canada. Now it goes to the people with a plebiscite and asks for an expression of opinion merely on the conscription of man-power. People are having their lives restricted by these orders in council in a way they scarcely dreamed of a short time ago. The cost of living is frozen; wages are frozen at a lower level, and agricultural products are frozen at a still lower level. The cost of production on the farm continues to increase, but the value the farmer will get for his products is frozen. What is happening is this: you are freezing servitude on labour and peasantry on the farmer. Sons are being taken from the farms; mortgage and loan companies are foreclosing and driving the parents off the land.
On February 1 a delegation will arrive in this city from the west, to protest even, in these times of strife, against this treatment. These people do not ask for profits; they merely ask that they be allowed to continue to work their farms and produce the foodstuffs so urgently needed both now and for the period of reconstruction. Britain is severely rationed to-day. Our Department of Agriculture says, "Grow less wheat and help win the war." Food is going to be needed as it has never been needed before. Those engaged in agriculture

in Canada wish to make their contribution. They wish to. be allowed to continue to make their sacrifice and do their bit to help save Canada.
In the west, as in other parts of Canada, the people turned to cooperatives as a means of protecting themselves against exploitation by the privileged who were stealing the substance of their production. They found that the banking institutions and the loan, mortgage and insurance companies were bleeding them white. The packing companies amassed their millions out of the unprotected producer and unorganized consumer. Implement and oil companies continued to charge what they wished. The grain exchange continued to steal its millions, yes, hundreds of millions from the producers. So the people organized themselves cooperatively.
In Saskatchewan the cooperative pool elevator company own over a thousand elevators which they use to handle their own grain, and they reached the point where they were handling almost fifty per cent of the grain produced in that province. But what happened? For two crop delivery seasons the car allotment committee, set up under the government grain board, effectively forced the producers to use the old line elevator companies and deliver their wheat to those companies and, through them, to the grain exchange. No cars could be obtained by the pool elevators beyond the allotment, which was based on the permanent storage capacity. To meet this regulation, the pools built temporary storage. This took them through 1940 fairly well, and they were planning to do the same thing for 1941; but the building of temporary storage, which had saved the pools the year before fairly well, was stopped by order of the lumber controller, and the cooperative organization was crippled. In many places it had to close its doors for months during the delivery season. Tens of millions of bushels of wheat, were thus directed through the old private and corporate business institutions, and through their channels to the grain exchange. Government agencies of this administration directly or indirectly effectively prevented the cooperative institutions from operating.
The people of Canada resent this deeply. Special privileged groups in the economic life of Canada have kept on exploiting the resources of this dominion to the point where the situation can no longer toe tolerated. The people of Canada will not permit their cooperative institutions to toe ruined in this way -and that goes for all of Canada. It goes for the Okanagan apple growers in British Columbia, for the western wheat farmers,

The Address-Mr. Castleden
for those who produce the cattle and beef, for t-hose who provide materials and food stuff. It goes for the cooperatives in Ontario and Quebec; it goes for the cooperatives in Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces.
This delegation of over 400 people coming here under the organization of the Saskatchewan wheat pools are coming to protest against the treatment of agriculture, and particularly against the treatment of western grain growers. Farmers across Canada have not been sufficiently well organized to make effective protest, and certain forces for years have been working to keep them from organizing. People do not come down here in war time for pleasure; they are not coming here to cause trouble. These are patriotic Canadians of good character. They are people who have fought and suffered, people who have helped build Canada. They are protesting against the treatment of agriculture, and they would not come here if conditions were not desperate. Those conditions are desperate. This administration has turned a deaf ear to the voices of these people, or those who spoke for them. One after another, ministers of agriculture in this house have betrayed the people of the west, and far too often have broken their pledges. Saskatchewan is withering and dying on account of the failure of this government to provide adequate legislation to protect the people of Saskatchewan.
Recent figures from the bureau of statistics show that the population of that province is decreasing from year to year. People just cannot exist out there. They are driven away from their province; they are driven off their homes. They are driven off the farms on which they have lived for possibly twenty or thirty years. This is the reward meted out by the administration to a people who have produced by billions the wealth of this dominion. They are a betrayed people.
This delegation coming to Ottawa is a living symbol in protest of that betrayal. People and homes are more important than profits. That should have been recognized in peace time; it should be recognized more fully in war time. Mothers' sons are more important than profits, and that should be recognized now. That delegation is coming here to speak for the masses in agriculture; it is marching here with a bill of rights; the government cannot disregard them. This is a demand for justice, and they are bringing it to the foot of the throne. That demand is coming from about two million people. Donations of dimes and quarters, a few dozen eggs, a few pounds of butter, or a chicken were made. And 160,000 or more people have signed their names to a petition of protest to the government. I would sug-14561-12
gest that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), who was associated with the grain growers institutions for some years, might explain to them the great battle which is being fought for them. I wish Mr. Dunning were here to speak to them, and I would be pleased if the ex-Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Motherwell, could do so. I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in the present government will hear these people, and the justice of their cause. They come asking for bread.

To return to the problem of reconstruction. During November 1 had the privilege of visiting an area in Canada where men of vision are providing leadership in a real way. I refer to that small university known as St. Francis Xavier in Antigonish, Nova Scotia. Through its extension department it has taken education to the masses of the people. When education went to the people light dawned and fear disappeared. They caught the vision of a better land; they learned that they could run their own institutions. Miners and fishermen, farmers and steel workers are running their own businesses, doing their own financing, operating their own packing plants, and in a cooperative way building their own houses. They have consumers' cooperatives, producers' cooperatives and wholesale cooperatives. For the first time they are learning the meaning of the word "exploitation." They are learning what is wrong with the plight of the common man, and how the fruit of his labour is stolen from him.
These people have learned about a system which has displaced profits as a motivating force. Cooperation must displace competition as a way of life. Service for one's fellow man is more efficient as a motive than profits for the few. Cooperation creates character, whereas competition destroys it. Cooperation builds the character of those who work with it, but competition born of the jungle, ruins, with poverty and slums, the exploited toilers and with corruption of too much wealth, those who steal from the workers.
Cooperation has created a vision of a society where economic security can reign, and with it democracy can live. Those people, marching forward, have a vision of a world in which Canada can make its contribution, a world where profit shall cease. Peace will be possible, because some day the profits of war will be eliminated. And when the profits of war are eliminated throughout the world, that curse which now returns to us every twenty j'ears will cease.

The Address-Mr. Castleden

To get the necessary morale established in Canada I would ask the government to do a few things. Immediately it should establish courageously and boldly some equality of sacrifice. It should start now with the conscription of industry and accumulated wealth. Then it would have some right to ask mothers to place their sons on the altar of national sacrifice. Place agriculture on a basis where it can play its part. Give to labour that degree of democracy it should have. Give Canada a vision of a reconstructed land where social justice shall reign, and economic security shall drive fear from the hearts of our people. This will give us the morale for victory which, I say, does not exist to-day.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak at this time may I be permitted to join those who have previously spoken in paying my compliments to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
We are going through momentous days; we are facing grave problems, we are almost at the turn of the way. I should like to read an excerpt from page 45 of Hansard of last Monday with respect to the war effort. It is:
These demands will intimately affect the lives of many men and women. They will also effect ^	nation in the following way:
there will be a further very definite curtailment of the amenities we have hitherto been able to preserve. These demands will not affect physical health or that contentment of spirit that comes from serving great causes, but they will make further inroads upon the comfort and convenience of very large numbers, and upon the character and aspect of our daily life.
It must not be supposed that there are large reserves of idle people leading a leisurely existence who can now be called to the national ranks. The entire adult Canadian population, with very few exceptions, gets up in the morning, works all day, and goes to bed tired out at night. In our form of society people have been accustomed to find their own jobs to a very large extent, thus saving vast government machinery.
If all the efforts of everyone were really devoted solely to making war, there would be no food, or fuel, no transport, or clothes. We have to recognize the fact that a very large proportion of the population, particularly women, is occupied in ministering to the needs of the more actively engaged population, and that that number has increased since the last war with the increase of population who have to be ministered to.
The process which is now to be applied-and has, indeed, been continuously applied-much more vigorously, is not the calling of idle people to work, hut the sharpening and shifting forward of a proportion of their effort into work which is more directly related to the war.
Those are the words of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) repeating the words of the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, Prime Minister of England. I

commend them to this parliament. The morale of the public of Canada was referred to by the previous speaker, and this feeling is echoed through this chamber and throughout the length and breadth of Canada. How many of the amenities of life has this government asked the Canadian people to forego in order that we may have a national all-out war effort? How many inroads have been made into the comforts and expenditures of our people? What has been done to take up the reserves of idle people? Since coming into .this house this session, we have heard hon. members from western Canada say that unemployment is still plentiful in that part of the country, and then we have heard hon. members from eastern Canada, particularly from agricultural constituencies, tell us of the need for farm labour. But we have not heard any policy announced by this government to cope with the situation. The service rendered by the women of Canada in administering to the needs of the unfortunate, in caring for the sick and wounded of our fighting forces, is well worthy of the Canadian morale. The war effort of these women has been performed valiantly and with a devotion to duty. As Mr. Churchill said, the process which is now being applied is to be more vigorously applied.
A number of our members have been overseas, and they have come back and told us of what they saw. We have heard of the shortage of agricultural products, of those things of which we have such a surplus. How much of this has been brought home to the Canadian people? What has been done to make the Canadian citizen sensitive to his or her responsibilities? What has been done to increase the cooperation between our citizens and those who are fighting to stem the tide of war away from our continent?
In the speech from the throne we are told that it is now proposed that a plebiscite shall be taken to grant pardon or absolution to the Prime Minister and to the government for promises made before the last election. A lot of water has flown under the mill since the last election. Times have changed since then. What will be the morale of the Canadian people; what will be the condition in Canada when this vote is taken? If this plebiscite is taken, it will probably be around the first of April, although the date has not yet been, announced. Do we know what the state of the world will be by April 1? Do we know what will have happened in Singapore by that date? In what condition will Australia be by April 1? What about New Zealand and the Philippines? What will Hitler and his hordes be doing in Asia and Africa? What

The Address-Mr. Boucher
will our kinsmen in England, Ireland and Scotland be doing? They are now facing a dire situation. The German and Italian hordes will probably be attempting an invasion of their country. In what mood will the people of Canada be to vote upon a plebiscite to release the Prime Minister, to grant absolution for a wrong? Obviously it was a wrong commitment.
If that commitment was not wrong, why this plebiscite? The Prime Minister has stated that the one point at issue in the plebiscite is the question of compulsory military service for overseas. If compulsory service for overseas is not necessary now, why the plebiscite? If compulsory service for overseas is necessary, when will the relief from that restriction be brought into effect and we in Canada be given an opportunity to do our whole part in this war? As I say, this plebiscite cannot be taken until on in April. The soldier is entitled to vote. How long will it be before a complete record of the plebiscite reaches Ottawa?
Assuming that the plebiscite is one hundred per cent satisfactory to the Prime Minister and his government, how long will it take them to put the machinery of compulsory service overseas into operation? Will he put it into operation? How long will it be before the men will be ready to commence training? How long will it take to make a soldier capable of serving overseas? When we look at things from that perspective, and consider that length of time, we can only come to the conclusion that it will be into next winter before we shall have results. Anything can happen between now and then.
What is this plebiscite? The Prime Minister has stated to the house, as reported at page 51 of Hansard, that the plebiscite is going to be worded thus:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
His statement to this house was that such was the bone of contention. Is the plebiscite being placed before the Canadian people to ask them if they are in favour of sending men by compulsory selection overseas? Is that what this plebiscite states? Why does he not ask parliament, and not the people, is it in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men? The plebiscite states "for military service." It does not say "overseas service". What is the answer to that question? Is it not asking this question: Are you willing to exonerate the Prime Minister and the government from
44561-121	'	.
any commitments they ever made in any manner with respect to sending men into the military forces?
The people of Canada are to be asked that question at one of the most critical times that you and I, Mr. Speaker, or any other member of this house could conceive, of. If that plebiscite is necessary, if any pardon is necessary, we have here in this House of Commons 245 members elected, with great responsibility, to do a terrific task and to represent the people who sent us to parliament.
What are the duties of the private member of this house? They are certainly not to formulate policy. Our task, to judge by the past performance of this administration, is not to pass legislation, because we sat here for thirteen days in November without any legislation before us. The principal policy announced in the speech from the throne this session is that the country be asked to forgive the government for its past commitments with respect to raising men. We had the priceceiling legislation passed a few days before parliament was called into session and we have orders in council passed every day whether parliament is sitting or not. What better authority can I quote than the Prime Minister himself for my statement that parliament should decide this question? I shall quote passages from statements made by the Prime Minister as far back as March 30, 1939, when speaking in this house he said, as reported at page 2612 of Hansard:
If Canada is faced by the necessity of making a decision on the most se.rious and momentous issue that can face a nation, whether or not to take part in war, the principle of responsible , government which has been our guide and our goal for a century past, demands that that decision be made by the parliament of Canada.
Again, from the same page:
Whether it has been in reference to the application of sanctions under Article 16 of the covenant of the league or to participation in wars apart altogether from the league, Canada's position has been the same, namely, that in either case the approval of parliament will be required.
Again!
The Canadian parliament reserves to itself the right to declare, in the light of the circumstances existing at the time, to what extent, if at all, Canada will participate in conflicts in which other members of the commonwealth may be engaged.
Again the Prime Minister comes back with the same thing on the same day, as reported at page 2618 of Hansard:
My immediate purpose in quoting the statement, as will be apparent from the context, was to emphasize the continuity of Liberal policy as regards parliamentary control, the view which was held then and which we as a
The Address-Mr. Boucher

government hold to-day, that in the great as in the small issues of a nation's policy, the policy of self-government which we have followed for a century makes it essential that parliament and no other body should decide.
Yet the policy for a century must now be discarded and this question referred to the people of Canada!
Again, as reported at page 48 of Hansard of Monday last the Prime Minister said!:
If the issue of conscription for service overseas is to be fought out, the place for it to be fought out is on the floor of this parliament.
Again, as reported at page 49 he said:
In a world situation so involved, with enemies on every front, with no one able to say what the outcome of battle in other parts of the world may bring of immediate and increased danger to our own land, the government feels strongly that it should be perfectly free to recommend to parliament whatever course of action it deems essential to the security of our own country, and to the preservation of freedom in our own and other lands.
I quote these passages to show that in this parliament some responsibility must be assumed by the members, some questions of national import must be dealt with, some duties must be performed. Is it not our duty to deal with the question raised in this plebiscite? But instead we have a plebiscite by which the people are asked to decide.
What is the purpose of the plebiscite in any event? What would happen if the plebiscite were answered in the negative? Will the government stop raising men? Will it stop using compulsion to raise them? Will it stop using the selective system? Will it go to the enemy and ask forgiveness, saying: "We meant to declare war, but we did not mean to raise men to fight that war." What would happen if some sections of our country vote overwhelmingly "yes", and some other sections overwhelmingly "no"? Will the government still claim to be the champion of national unity? Will the government still feel that to preserve national unity they must take no course at all lest they offend either the yeas or the nays? Why does not the Prime Minister in his plebiscite put this further question to the Canadian people: Are you in favour of the plebiscite being taken at all at this time? If he wants to interpret the plebiscite as an endorsation of his policy and as approval of his administration, what better question could he ask? If the Prime Minister has any doubt as to whether the people of Canada will release him from his pledges-and he does not seem to have any- why not find out from their elected representatives in this parliament whose duty it is to reflect the opinions of the people, and let us get on with the war? Possibly the

answer should be the formation of a government under a man who is not manacled or handicapped by his previous commitments. What was his answer to that? I hesitate to repeat what I interpret it to be. As reported at page 31 of Hansard, in dealing with that very question he said:
In other words, I am being asked to "sell my birthright for their mess of pottage", and to destroy whatever confidence the people of Canada may possess in my honour as a public man, and, in doing so, also to destroy the confidence the people possess in the honour and integrity of the government.
Are we still in the days of the Tudor kings, of the Jameses, and of the policy of the divine right of kings, or has it just come down to the divine right of King?
Apart, however, from the wisdom, the folly or the blunder of a plebiscite at this time, I should like to express what I take to be the opinion of the agriculturists in my riding. The fanners of my riding are to a large extent men operating farms of from 100 to 400 acres. Their pursuits are the dairying industry, the hog industry, the beef industry, and egg production. Like most farmers, for the last ten or fifteen years they have gone through very difficult times. Many of the farms have been left idle. Within the last few years, conditions, through the increased demands for their supplies, and through federal and provincial government subsidies of one kind or another, have greatly improved. They have not sufficiently improved, however, to attract to' the farms the help which is required, or to keep on the farms the men who are already there. Go through the rural centres in eastern Ontario and look for young people, and you will find that many of our rural centres are like Goldsmith's deserted village. School attendance has greatly decreased from what it has been at any time within the past twenty years. Aggravating this condition is the policy of calling to the armed forces farmers' sons and farm help upon short notice. Repeatedly and almost constantly I have found agricultural workers being called for military training and given ten days to apply for postponement when seven or eight of the ten days have already elapsed before the notice is received. It is annoying and, I say, alarming to see how many boys are being called for military service when they are the sole persons running the farm or the main help on that farm, and are totally indispensable to the production of milk, cheese, beef, bacon and eggs.
When national registration was taken, information was given to the military authorities and to the government to indicate what

The Address-Mr. Boucher
men were available with least impairment of our war effort. The Prime Minister has himself stated that agriculture is a very essential part of our war effort. Something will have to be done to provide labour in view of the increasing demand for food, involving greater production. If that is the situation, and if this information has been made available through national registration, why should men have been called up who are the only help on the , farm and where they are essential to necessary agricultural production? Truly, postponements can be granted. To my own knowledge many have been granted. But any man who appreciates the problems of the farmer will realize the difficulties of putting in a crop, of growing the produce required, without some assurance as to the help which will be obtainable for reaping it. The farmer must plant1 his crop from the viewpoint of the available help, not at present, but six months, a year, or even two years ahead. Many farmers to-day, even within twenty miles of this capital city, are being compelled to reduce their stock, and even to quit their occupation, on account of shortage of help. I believe that this essential part of our farm problem, coupled with our war problems, should long before now have been taken into consideration by parliament. A broad and comprehensive scheme of calling men to military service in some order, with some certainty, should have been placed before our people. It may not be possible under such a scheme to state just when a certain man is going to be called, but the order in which men are to be called in relation to their occupations should be announced. I believe it is the policy of the government to call up men in accordance with age and1 marital status. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the occupation of a man in civilian life is an important factor. If a man is engaged in a productive capacity in an essential war industry, that point should be taken into consideration, and he should have some certainty as to the necessity of his appearing for military training, and as to those who should appear before he does.
Any man who has knowledge of the agricultural industry-and there are few here who have not-will realize the amount of foresight and planning required to produce the products which are so essential to our requirements, and how difficult it will be, under the present policy of this government, for a farmer owning anywhere from 20 to 160 head of cattle, as is the case with many in my riding, to operate his farm if his son or his hired man is called for military service, given ten days to apply for postponement, and does not know until, perhaps, two or three days before the time for reporting, whether
he is to report or whether the postponement is granted. What is the farmer to do if postponement is not granted, when help cannot be had? If postponement is granted, it is to the first of April, the first of May, or the first of July-right at the busiest time. No wonder agriculturists are very much discontented; no wonder our production is not what it should be, when consideration in such matters as this is not given to our agriculturists. Remembering that we are in the third year of the war, I believe the time is long past when a broad and comprehensive scheme of calling men to the service should be placed before the country. If the time when certain individuals are likely to be called to service cannot be announced, the order in which men are to be called in relation to their occupation should be made known. The age group and the marital status should not be the only order of calling.
I believe that for a total war effort there is plenty of work within the confines of the army, the navy and the air force for men of almost every possible classification of health and physical condition, and in my opinion these matters should long before now have been taken into consideration and placed before the people. Back of information along this line has caused a great deal of dissatisfaction among our people, who are anxious to have some guidance in these matters. If it is necessary to prepare for the shortage of sugar, as announced in to-day's papers,, or for the shortage of gasoline, which has been talked about for three or four months in advance, why is it not equally important to consider the primary industry of agriculture, and why is it not equally important to discuss or to consider the necessity of getting our man-power armed, trained, equipped and placed for service overseas?
On motion of Mr. Pouliot the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
